title: Where SQL fits in data engineering
md:
By the end of this chapter you can explain where SQL sits in a data platform, name the five practice tables you'll use all course, and run your first queries on them. ## Why a data engineer lives in SQL A data engineer moves data from where it's created to where it's trusted. Python and Spark do some of the moving. Almost everything else is SQL: - **Checking what arrived.** Did today's file have the usual number of rows? Are there new NULLs? - **Cleaning and shaping.** Turning raw events into clean tables, one row per order or per customer per day. - **Modelling.** Facts and dimensions that analysts can query without knowing how the source works. - **Loading.** INSERT, MERGE and overwrite patterns that don't double count. - **Debugging.** When a dashboard number looks wrong, you trace it back with queries. Spark SQL, Databricks SQL, Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Postgres and DuckDB all speak SQL. dbt models are SQL files. Learn SQL well once and it works everywhere, with small dialect differences (chapter 19). ## The life of one order Follow one food order from the app to a dashboard: | Step | System | Shape of the data | |---|---|---| | 1. You tap "Place order" | App database (OLTP), e.g. Postgres | One row in `orders`, updated as the status changes | | 2. The change is captured | CDC tool or a nightly export | A file or event per change | | 3. It lands in the lake | Cloud storage (S3, ADLS, GCS) | Raw JSON or CSV, untouched (bronze) | | 4. It's cleaned | Spark or a warehouse | Typed, deduplicated rows (silver) | | 5. It's modelled | SQL models, often dbt | Facts and dimensions (gold) | | 6. Someone reads it | BI tool, notebook, API | "Revenue by city yesterday" | Steps 4 to 6 are mostly SQL. Step 1 is SQL too, but a different kind. ## OLTP and OLAP: two kinds of database | | OLTP (the app's database) | OLAP (warehouse or lakehouse) | |---|---|---| | Job | Run the business: place an order, update a status | Understand the business: revenue by month | | Typical query | Read or write one row by its key | Scan millions of rows, aggregate a few columns | | Storage | Row by row | Column by column (Parquet, Delta, Iceberg) | | Design | Normalised: many small tables, no repeats | Denormalised for reading: facts and dimensions | | Examples | Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server | Databricks, Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, DuckDB | A data engineer reads from OLTP systems and builds OLAP ones. Never run a heavy analytics query on the app's production database: you can slow down checkout for real customers. ## Meet your practice tables Every example in this course runs in your browser on the Playground's shop data: about 2.6 million rows, generated the same for everyone. Press **Run it** on any SQL block to open it in the Playground. | Table | Rows | One row is | Mess added on purpose | |---|---|---|---| | `shop_customers` | 100,000 | a customer | about 2% have no city, 3% no email | | `shop_products` | 5,000 | a product | none | | `shop_orders` | 1,000,000 | an order line, 2024 to 2025 | statuses include cancelled and returned | | `web_events` | 1,000,000 | a click on the website or app | 1% duplicated events, 20% anonymous users | | `taxi_trips` | 500,000 | a cab trip | zero distances, negative fares | The **grain** (what one row means) is the most important fact about any table. Say it out loud before you write a query. ## Your first queries Look at a few rows before anything else: ```sql SELECT * FROM shop_orders LIMIT 10; ``` See the columns and their types: ```sql DESCRIBE shop_orders; ``` Count the rows, and see the date range: ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, MIN(order_ts) AS first_order, MAX(order_ts) AS last_order FROM shop_orders; ``` ## Profile a table in one query When a new table lands, data engineers profile it: how many rows, how many distinct keys, how many NULLs. This one query tells you a lot about `shop_customers`: ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS distinct_ids, COUNT(*) - COUNT(city) AS missing_city, COUNT(*) - COUNT(email) AS missing_email, MIN(signup_date) AS first_signup, MAX(signup_date) AS last_signup FROM shop_customers; ``` If `distinct_ids` is less than `row_count`, the key isn't unique and every join on it will multiply rows. You'll see why in chapter 5. ## How to read the rest of this course Each chapter has the same shape: the idea, worked examples you can run, the mistakes people make, what interviewers ask, a quick check, and lab problems to practise on. Type the examples yourself rather than only pressing Run: your fingers learn SQL faster than your eyes do. ## Common mistakes - **Querying before knowing the grain.** "Revenue per customer" from an order-line table needs a SUM. From a customer table it's a lookup. - **Running heavy queries on the app's database.** Use a replica, an export, or the warehouse. - **Trusting a table because it exists.** Profile it first: row count, key uniqueness, NULLs, date range. ## In the interview **"How do you use SQL day to day?"** A strong answer names real tasks: "I write the transformations from raw to clean tables, the MERGE that loads them, and the quality checks that run before a dashboard refreshes. When numbers look wrong, SQL is how I trace them back." **Follow-up: "What's the difference between OLTP and OLAP?"** OLTP runs the business, with row-at-a-time reads and writes. OLAP analyses it, with column scans over millions of rows. Then say why it matters: you design tables differently for each. ```quiz What is the grain of `shop_orders`? - One row per customer * One row per order line - One row per day > The grain is what one row means. Each row of shop_orders is one order line, so "orders per customer" needs a COUNT grouped by customer. --- `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` is lower than `COUNT(*)` in a customer table. What does that tell you? - The table has NULL customer ids only * Some customer ids appear more than once, so joins on it will multiply rows - Nothing, that's normal for a customer table > A customer table should have one row per customer. Duplicated keys mean every join on customer_id can multiply rows. --- Why shouldn't you run a big analytics query on the app's production database? - SQL works differently there * It competes with real customers' queries and can slow the app down - OLTP databases can't run GROUP BY > OLTP databases are tuned for many small reads and writes. A big scan can slow down checkout. Use a replica or the warehouse. ```
Practise thisOpen the Playground and profile shop_productsSQL 70Logical order of execution of a SELECT

title: Data types and table design
md:
By the end of this chapter you can pick the right type for every column, explain why money is never a float, and design a table with sensible keys and constraints. ## Why types matter A type is a promise about what a column holds. Get it right and the engine stores data compactly, sorts it correctly and catches bad values. Get it wrong and you get wrong totals, slow joins, or dates that sort as text: "2026-10-9" comes after "2026-10-10". ## The types you'll use most | Kind | Types | Use for | Watch out | |---|---|---|---| | Whole numbers | `INTEGER`, `BIGINT` | ids, counts, quantities | INTEGER tops out near 2.1 billion. Use BIGINT for event ids. | | Exact decimals | `DECIMAL(p, s)` / `NUMERIC` | money, rates you report | `p` is total digits, `s` is digits after the point | | Approximate | `DOUBLE`, `FLOAT`, `REAL` | measurements, scores, ML features | never for money: binary rounding errors | | Text | `VARCHAR`, `STRING`, `TEXT` | names, codes, free text | trailing spaces and case make "equal" values differ | | Dates and times | `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP`, `TIMESTAMPTZ` | events, business dates | store UTC, convert at the edge (chapter 10) | | True or false | `BOOLEAN` | flags like `is_premium` | NULL is a third state, not false | | Nested | `ARRAY`/`LIST`, `STRUCT`, `MAP`, `JSON` | events and API payloads | flatten before you join (chapter 12) | ## Why money is never a float Floats store numbers in binary, and most decimal fractions can't be written exactly in binary. Try it: ```sql SELECT 0.1::DOUBLE + 0.2::DOUBLE AS float_sum, 0.1::DOUBLE + 0.2::DOUBLE = 0.3::DOUBLE AS float_equal, 0.1::DECIMAL(10,2) + 0.2::DECIMAL(10,2) = 0.3 AS decimal_equal; ``` `float_equal` is false. Across a million order lines these tiny errors add up, and finance's total won't match yours. In the practice tables, `unit_price` is `DECIMAL(10,2)` for exactly this reason. ## Casting: changing a value's type `CAST(x AS type)` (or `x::type` in DuckDB, Postgres and Spark) converts a value. When the value can't convert, `CAST` raises an error, which stops a pipeline. `TRY_CAST` returns NULL instead, so you can catch and quarantine the bad rows: ```sql SELECT raw, TRY_CAST(raw AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS as_is, TRY_CAST(regexp_replace(raw, '[^0-9.]', '', 'g') AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS cleaned FROM (VALUES ('349.00'), ('₹349.00'), ('three hundred'), (NULL)) AS t(raw); ``` The pattern above is a real one: raw text comes in, a cleaned version goes to silver, and rows where `cleaned` is still NULL go to a quarantine table with a reason. > Spark and Databricks with ANSI mode on (the default on serverless) also raise errors on bad casts. Use `try_cast`, `try_to_timestamp` and `try_divide` there. ## Keys - **Primary key:** the column (or columns) that identify a row. In `shop_orders` it's `order_id`. - **Natural key:** a key from the business, like an email or a GST number. It can change. - **Surrogate key:** a meaningless id you generate, like `customer_sk = 1, 2, 3…`. It never changes, which is why dimensions use one (chapter 14). - **Foreign key:** a column that points at another table's key, like `shop_orders.customer_id`. Warehouses and lakehouses (Databricks, Snowflake, BigQuery) usually **don't enforce** primary and foreign keys. You can declare them, but the engine won't stop a duplicate. Your pipeline and your quality checks have to do it (chapter 18). ## Designing a table Here's a cleaned orders table as a data engineer would design it: ```sql CREATE TABLE silver_orders ( order_id BIGINT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL, product_id INTEGER NOT NULL, order_ts TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, -- when it happened (UTC) order_date DATE NOT NULL, -- derived, for filters and partitions quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0), unit_price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price >= 0), discount_pct INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (discount_pct BETWEEN 0 AND 100), status VARCHAR NOT NULL, _source_file VARCHAR, -- where the row came from _ingested_at TIMESTAMP -- when we loaded it ); ``` Choices worth defending in an interview: - **`NOT NULL` on everything the business needs.** A NULL quantity is a bug, so the table refuses it. - **`CHECK` constraints** catch impossible values at write time. - **A derived `order_date`** makes daily filters and partitioning simple. - **Audit columns** (`_source_file`, `_ingested_at`) let you trace any row back to its file, which you'll want at 3 AM. ## Create a table from a query Most tables in a pipeline are created from a query (CTAS, "create table as select"): ```sql CREATE TABLE daily_revenue AS SELECT CAST(order_ts AS DATE) AS order_date, SUM(quantity * unit_price * (1 - discount_pct / 100.0)) AS revenue FROM shop_orders WHERE status = 'delivered' GROUP BY 1; SELECT * FROM daily_revenue ORDER BY order_date LIMIT 5; ``` ## Common mistakes - **Dates stored as text.** They sort wrong and can't be compared. Cast once, in silver. - **Money as FLOAT or DOUBLE.** Use DECIMAL with enough digits: `DECIMAL(18,2)` covers almost any total. - **Joining INTEGER to VARCHAR.** Some engines cast silently and scan everything, others fail. Make key types match. - **INTEGER ids for events.** A busy app passes 2.1 billion events quickly. Use BIGINT. - **Assuming the warehouse enforces keys.** It usually doesn't. Check uniqueness yourself. ## In the interview **"Design a table for orders."** Start with the grain ("one row per order line"), then the key, then the types, especially DECIMAL for money and TIMESTAMP in UTC. Then constraints and audit columns. Say what you'd partition or cluster by (order date). **Follow-up: "Natural or surrogate key?"** Natural keys can change and can come from several systems. A surrogate key is stable and makes SCD Type 2 history possible. Keep the natural key as a column too, so you can join back to the source. ```quiz Which type should hold `unit_price`? - DOUBLE * DECIMAL(10,2) - VARCHAR > Money needs exact decimal arithmetic. DOUBLE has binary rounding errors, and VARCHAR can't be summed. --- A raw column holds values like "₹349.00" and "N/A". What's the safest way to turn it into a number in a pipeline? - CAST(raw AS DECIMAL(10,2)) * Strip the symbols, TRY_CAST, and quarantine rows that come back NULL - Leave it as text and cast in the dashboard > CAST would fail the whole job on the first bad value. TRY_CAST lets you keep the good rows and send the bad ones somewhere you can look at them. --- Databricks lets you declare a primary key on a table. What happens if you insert a duplicate? * It's accepted. The key is informational, so you must check uniqueness yourself - The insert fails - The old row is replaced > Most warehouses and lakehouses treat primary and foreign keys as information for the optimizer and for people, not as rules they enforce. ```

title: Querying fundamentals
md:
By the end of this chapter you can filter, sort, compute and label rows, and you know the order in which the engine actually runs a query, which explains most beginner errors. ## The shape of a query ```sql SELECT customer_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(quantity * unit_price) > 50000 ORDER BY gross DESC LIMIT 10; ``` That's the top 10 customers by gross spend in 2025, among those who spent more than ₹50,000. Each clause has one job. ## The order the engine runs it You write SELECT first, but the engine runs it almost last: 1. `FROM` and `JOIN`: build the rows 2. `WHERE`: keep some rows 3. `GROUP BY`: form groups 4. `HAVING`: keep some groups 5. `SELECT`: compute the output columns, including window functions 6. `DISTINCT`: remove duplicate output rows 7. `ORDER BY`: sort 8. `LIMIT` / `OFFSET`: cut This explains three rules that confuse beginners: - **You can't use a SELECT alias in WHERE.** WHERE runs before SELECT, so the alias doesn't exist yet. (DuckDB is friendlier and allows it, but don't rely on that in interviews.) - **You can't put an aggregate in WHERE.** Groups don't exist yet. Use HAVING. - **You can't put a window function in WHERE.** Windows are computed in SELECT. Wrap the query, or use QUALIFY (chapter 9). ## Selecting and computing ```sql SELECT order_id, quantity, unit_price, discount_pct, quantity * unit_price AS gross, quantity * unit_price * (1 - discount_pct / 100.0) AS net FROM shop_orders LIMIT 5; ``` Note `/ 100.0` and not `/ 100`. In Postgres and SQL Server, an integer divided by an integer is an integer: `15 / 100` is `0`, and every discount would vanish. DuckDB, Spark, Snowflake and BigQuery return a fraction there, but writing `100.0` makes your SQL correct everywhere. ## Filtering with WHERE ```sql SELECT order_id, order_ts, status, payment_method, channel FROM shop_orders WHERE status IN ('delivered', 'shipped') AND payment_method = 'UPI' AND channel <> 'marketplace' AND order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-03-01' AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01' LIMIT 20; ``` The operators you'll use daily: | Operator | Example | Note | |---|---|---| | `=`, `<>` (or `!=`) | `status = 'delivered'` | text is case-sensitive in most engines | | `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` | `order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-03-01'` | | | `BETWEEN a AND b` | `quantity BETWEEN 2 AND 5` | inclusive on both ends | | `IN (...)` | `status IN ('shipped', 'delivered')` | a short list of values | | `LIKE`, `ILIKE` | `email LIKE '%@example.com'` | `%` any characters, `_` exactly one. ILIKE ignores case. | | `IS NULL`, `IS NOT NULL` | `city IS NULL` | `= NULL` never matches (chapter 4) | | `AND`, `OR`, `NOT` | | AND binds tighter than OR: use brackets | ## Half-open date ranges For a month of timestamps, use `>= start AND < next_start`: ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS march_orders FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-03-01' AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01'; ``` `BETWEEN '2025-03-01' AND '2025-03-31'` looks right but is wrong for timestamps: `'2025-03-31'` means midnight at the start of the 31st, so it drops almost a whole day of orders. Half-open ranges never overlap and never leave gaps, which is why pipelines use them for every incremental window. ## The AND/OR trap ```sql -- Wrong: means "UPI orders that are delivered" OR "any cancelled order" SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shop_orders WHERE payment_method = 'UPI' AND status = 'delivered' OR status = 'cancelled'; -- Right: brackets say what you mean SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shop_orders WHERE payment_method = 'UPI' AND (status = 'delivered' OR status = 'cancelled'); ``` Run both and compare the counts. Whenever you mix AND and OR, add brackets, even when you think you don't need them. ## Labelling with CASE CASE turns values into categories: ```sql SELECT order_id, quantity * unit_price AS gross, CASE WHEN quantity * unit_price >= 10000 THEN 'large' WHEN quantity * unit_price >= 1000 THEN 'medium' ELSE 'small' END AS order_size FROM shop_orders LIMIT 10; ``` CASE checks its branches top to bottom and stops at the first match, so put the strictest condition first. Without an ELSE, unmatched rows get NULL. ## Sorting, limiting and DISTINCT ```sql SELECT DISTINCT channel, payment_method FROM shop_orders ORDER BY channel, payment_method; ``` - `ORDER BY` can sort by several columns, each `ASC` (default) or `DESC`. - Without ORDER BY, row order is not guaranteed, not even between two runs of the same query. - `LIMIT 10` without ORDER BY gives you *some* 10 rows, not the first 10. - `DISTINCT` applies to the whole output row, not just the first column. ## Common mistakes - **Integer division.** `discount_pct / 100` is 0 in Postgres and SQL Server. Write `100.0`. - **BETWEEN on timestamps.** It drops most of the last day. Use half-open ranges. - **Mixing AND and OR without brackets.** - **`LIMIT` without `ORDER BY`** in a result someone will rely on. - **`SELECT *` in pipelines.** A new source column silently changes your table. Name the columns. ## In the interview **"In what order does SQL execute a query?"** FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. Then give a consequence: "That's why I can't filter on a window function in WHERE and need QUALIFY or a subquery." **Follow-up: "WHERE or HAVING?"** WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after. Filter in WHERE whenever you can: fewer rows reach the GROUP BY, so it's faster. ```quiz Why does `SELECT quantity * 2 AS q2 FROM t WHERE q2 > 10` fail in most engines? - Aliases can't contain digits * WHERE runs before SELECT, so the alias doesn't exist yet - WHERE can't compare numbers > Logical order: FROM, WHERE, then SELECT. Repeat the expression in WHERE, or wrap the query. --- You need all orders placed in March 2025. Which filter is correct for a TIMESTAMP column? - `order_ts BETWEEN '2025-03-01' AND '2025-03-31'` * `order_ts >= '2025-03-01' AND order_ts < '2025-04-01'` - `order_ts LIKE '2025-03%'` > BETWEEN stops at midnight at the start of 31 March. The half-open range covers every second of March. --- In Postgres, what does `15 / 100` return? * 0 - 0.15 - An error > Integer divided by integer is integer division in Postgres and SQL Server. Write 15 / 100.0. ```

title: NULL handling
md:
By the end of this chapter you can predict what any expression does with a NULL, and you can spot the three NULL bugs that quietly drop rows from real pipelines. ## What NULL means NULL is not zero, not an empty string and not "false". It means *unknown*. That one idea explains every rule below: if you don't know a value, you also don't know whether it equals something else. In the Playground, 1,954 customers have no city and 2,943 have no email. In web events, 199,538 rows have no user_id because the visitor never logged in. Real sources look like this every day. ## Three-valued logic Comparisons with NULL return NULL, not true or false: ```sql SELECT NULL = NULL AS eq, NULL <> 'Delhi' AS neq, NULL > 5 AS gt, NULL IS NULL AS is_null, NULL AND FALSE AS and_false, NULL OR TRUE AS or_true; ``` WHERE keeps a row only when the condition is TRUE. NULL is not TRUE, so the row is dropped. Note the last two: `NULL AND FALSE` is FALSE and `NULL OR TRUE` is TRUE, because the answer doesn't depend on the unknown part. ## Trap 1: `<>` silently drops NULLs "Customers outside Delhi" sounds simple: ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS not_delhi FROM shop_customers WHERE city <> 'Delhi'; ``` That returns 93,238. But 1,954 customers with no city are also "not in Delhi" as far as the business is concerned, and they vanished. Say what you mean: ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS not_delhi_incl_unknown FROM shop_customers WHERE city IS DISTINCT FROM 'Delhi'; ``` `IS DISTINCT FROM` treats NULL as a normal value: two NULLs are "not distinct", and NULL is distinct from 'Delhi'. It works in DuckDB, Postgres, Spark, Databricks and Snowflake. Spark also has the operator `<=>` for null-safe equality. In engines without it, write `(city <> 'Delhi' OR city IS NULL)`. ## Trap 2: NOT IN with a NULL in the list Which customers never visited the website? ```sql -- Returns 0 rows. Why? SELECT COUNT(*) AS never_visited FROM shop_customers WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM web_events); ``` `x NOT IN (a, b, NULL)` means `x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL`. The last part is NULL, so the whole condition can never be TRUE. One anonymous event wipes out the whole answer. Use NOT EXISTS, which doesn't have this problem: ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS never_visited FROM shop_customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM web_events e WHERE e.user_id = c.customer_id ); ``` That returns 140. Make NOT EXISTS (or an anti join, chapter 5) your default. If you must use NOT IN, add `WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery. ## Trap 3: aggregates skip NULLs ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(email) AS with_email, COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS distinct_cities FROM shop_customers; ``` `COUNT(*)` counts rows. `COUNT(col)` counts non-NULL values. SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX ignore NULLs too, which changes averages: ```sql SELECT AVG(score) AS avg_ignoring_null, AVG(COALESCE(score, 0)) AS avg_null_as_zero FROM (VALUES (10), (20), (NULL)) AS t(score); ``` The first is 15, the second is 10. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. Decide which one the business means and write it down. ## Tools for NULLs | Function | What it does | Example | |---|---|---| | `COALESCE(a, b, ...)` | first non-NULL argument | `COALESCE(city, 'Unknown')` | | `NULLIF(a, b)` | NULL when a = b, else a | `clicks / NULLIF(views, 0)` avoids divide by zero | | `IS [NOT] NULL` | the only correct NULL test | `email IS NULL` | | `IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM` | null-safe comparison | `old.city IS DISTINCT FROM new.city` | | `IFNULL`, `NVL`, `ISNULL` | two-argument COALESCE in some dialects | prefer COALESCE, it works everywhere | ```sql SELECT customer_id, COALESCE(city, 'Unknown') AS city, COALESCE(email, 'missing') AS email FROM shop_customers WHERE city IS NULL OR email IS NULL LIMIT 10; ``` ## NULLs in joins, grouping and sorting - **Joins:** `a.key = b.key` never matches NULL keys, so rows with a NULL key drop out of inner joins. A LEFT JOIN keeps them but with NULLs on the right side. - **GROUP BY** puts all NULLs in one group. So does DISTINCT. - **ORDER BY:** where NULLs land depends on the engine. Write `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` when it matters. - **Change detection:** in a pipeline, `WHERE old.city <> new.city` misses a city going from NULL to 'Pune'. Always use `IS DISTINCT FROM` when comparing old and new rows. This is one of the most common real SCD bugs (chapter 14). ```sql SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customers FROM shop_customers GROUP BY city ORDER BY customers DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 5; ``` ## Common mistakes - **`= NULL`** instead of `IS NULL`. It never matches. - **`<>` on a nullable column** in a filter that should keep unknowns. - **`NOT IN` over a nullable subquery.** Returns nothing. - **Dividing by a column that can be 0.** Wrap it: `NULLIF(views, 0)`. - **COALESCE to a fake value** like `'1900-01-01'` in a fact table. It hides the gap from everyone downstream. Keep NULL and document it, or use an explicit "Unknown" member in a dimension. ## In the interview **"Why does `WHERE city <> 'Delhi'` miss some rows?"** Because NULL compared with anything is NULL, and WHERE keeps only TRUE. Fix it with `IS DISTINCT FROM` or `OR city IS NULL`. **"Why can NOT IN return no rows?"** One NULL in the subquery makes every `<>` comparison unknown. Use NOT EXISTS. Saying this unprompted, with the reason, is a strong signal in a DE interview. ```quiz What does `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE col = NULL` return when col has 50 NULLs? - 50 * 0 - An error > `col = NULL` is NULL for every row, and WHERE keeps only TRUE. Use `col IS NULL`. --- The subquery `SELECT user_id FROM web_events` contains NULLs. What does `WHERE id NOT IN (subquery)` return? - Only the ids that never appear * No rows at all - Every row > `id <> NULL` is unknown, so the whole NOT IN can never be TRUE. Use NOT EXISTS instead. --- Values are 10, 20 and NULL. What is AVG(value)? - 10 * 15 - NULL > AVG ignores NULLs, so it's (10 + 20) / 2. AVG(COALESCE(value, 0)) would be 10. ```
Practise thisSQL 74Trap: why does WHERE city <> 'Delhi' miss some rows?SQL 75Trap: why does NOT IN return no rows?SQL 72Trap: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) vs COUNT(DISTINCT col)SQL 66Null-count report for key columns in one passSQL 57Click-through rate per ad, without division errors

title: Joins
md:
By the end of this chapter you can pick the right join for any question, predict the row count before you run it, and catch the two join bugs that cause most wrong dashboards: fan-out and the LEFT JOIN filter trap. ## Why joins matter so much in DE Source systems store each thing once: customers in one table, products in another, orders pointing at both. Almost every pipeline step that builds something useful joins them back together. Get a join wrong and every number downstream is wrong, usually without an error. ## The join types | Join | Keeps | Use it for | |---|---|---| | `INNER JOIN` | only rows that match on both sides | enrich orders with customer details | | `LEFT JOIN` | every left row, matched right columns or NULL | "all customers, with their orders if any" | | `RIGHT JOIN` | every right row | rarely needed: swap the tables and use LEFT | | `FULL OUTER JOIN` | every row from both sides | reconciling source against target | | `CROSS JOIN` | every combination | building a date × product grid | | Semi join (`EXISTS`) | left rows that have a match, once each | "customers who ordered" | | Anti join (`NOT EXISTS`) | left rows with no match | "customers who never ordered" | ```sql SELECT o.order_id, o.order_ts, c.full_name, c.city, p.product_name, p.category FROM shop_orders o JOIN shop_customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN shop_products p ON p.product_id = o.product_id LIMIT 10; ``` Always alias tables and prefix every column. When a second table gains a column with the same name, unprefixed queries break. ## Predict the row count first Before running a join, say out loud how many rows you expect. Orders to customers is many-to-one, so an inner join keeps exactly one row per order: ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders_with_customer FROM shop_orders o JOIN shop_customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id; ``` That's 1,000,000, the same as the orders table, so no order lost its customer. A LEFT JOIN from customers to orders gives 1,000,049: one row per order plus one row for each of the 49 customers who never ordered. If the count is bigger than you expected, you have fan-out. ## Fan-out: the silent number inflater A join multiplies rows whenever the key repeats on the side you didn't expect. Here a small "targets" table accidentally has two rows for Mumbai: ```sql WITH city_targets(city, target) AS ( VALUES ('Mumbai', 100), ('Mumbai', 120), ('Pune', 80) ) SELECT c.city, COUNT(*) AS customer_rows_after_join FROM shop_customers c JOIN city_targets t ON t.city = c.city GROUP BY c.city ORDER BY c.city; ``` Every Mumbai customer now appears twice, so any SUM over that join doubles. Before joining, check that the key is unique on the side that should be "one": ```sql SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM shop_customers GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; ``` No rows back means customer_id is unique and safe to join on. ## The LEFT JOIN filter trap "All customers, with their count of cancelled orders, including zero": ```sql -- Wrong: the WHERE throws away customers with no cancelled orders SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c.customer_id) AS customers FROM shop_customers c LEFT JOIN shop_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'cancelled'; ``` For customers with no cancelled order, `o.status` is NULL, the WHERE drops them, and the LEFT JOIN has quietly become an INNER JOIN. Put conditions on the right-hand table in the ON clause: ```sql SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c.customer_id) AS customers, COUNT(o.order_id) AS cancelled_orders FROM shop_customers c LEFT JOIN shop_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'cancelled'; ``` Now every one of the 100,000 customers is kept. The rule: filters on the left table go in WHERE, filters on the right table of a LEFT JOIN go in ON. ## Semi and anti joins To ask "does a match exist?", don't join and DISTINCT. Use EXISTS: ```sql -- Customers who placed at least one UPI order SELECT COUNT(*) AS upi_customers FROM shop_customers c WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM shop_orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.payment_method = 'UPI' ); ``` ```sql -- Customers who never ordered: the anti join SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, c.signup_date FROM shop_customers c LEFT JOIN shop_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL ORDER BY c.signup_date DESC LIMIT 10; ``` The `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL` pattern and `NOT EXISTS` give the same result. Spark and DuckDB also accept `LEFT SEMI JOIN` and `LEFT ANTI JOIN`. ## Self joins and cross joins A self join compares rows in the same table, like "employees earning more than their manager" (practice 3). A cross join builds every combination, useful for filling gaps: ```sql WITH months AS ( SELECT * FROM (VALUES (DATE '2025-01-01'), (DATE '2025-02-01'), (DATE '2025-03-01')) m(month) ), cats AS ( SELECT DISTINCT category FROM shop_products ) SELECT m.month, c.category FROM months m CROSS JOIN cats c ORDER BY m.month, c.category; ``` Left join your real sales onto this grid and every month × category shows up, even with zero sales, which is what a chart needs. ## How engines run joins You'll meet these names in query plans and in the Spark chapters: - **Hash join:** build a hash table on the smaller side, stream the bigger side through it. The default for equality joins. - **Broadcast join** (Spark): copy the small table to every worker so the big one never moves. Fastest when one side is small. - **Sort-merge join:** sort both sides by the key, then walk them together. Spark's default for two big tables. - **Nested loop:** compare every pair. Used for non-equality conditions like `a.ts BETWEEN b.start AND b.end`. Slow on big tables. ## Common mistakes - **Not checking key uniqueness** before joining. Fan-out doubles revenue. - **Right-table filter in WHERE** after a LEFT JOIN. - **JOIN then DISTINCT** to fix duplicates. It hides fan-out instead of fixing the key. Use EXISTS. - **Joining on columns of different types**, like a string id against an integer id. Some engines cast silently and can't use indexes or partitions. - **NULL keys.** They never match, so those rows drop out of inner joins. ## In the interview **"Table A has 5 rows, table B has 3. How many rows does each join return?"** It depends on the keys, and saying so is the point. Walk through the matches: an inner join returns the matching pairs, a LEFT JOIN adds unmatched A rows, a FULL JOIN adds unmatched rows from both. With duplicate keys, matches multiply. Practice 7 drills exactly this. **"Customers who never ordered?"** Give NOT EXISTS or the LEFT JOIN / IS NULL anti join, and mention why NOT IN is risky with NULLs. ```quiz After `customers LEFT JOIN orders ... WHERE orders.status = 'cancelled'`, what happened to customers with no cancelled orders? - They are kept with NULL status * They are dropped, as if it were an inner join - The query errors > The WHERE runs after the join, and NULL = 'cancelled' isn't TRUE. Move the condition into ON. --- A revenue total doubled after you joined a targets table. What is the most likely cause? - The SUM function rounds up * The join key repeats in the targets table, so rows fan out - LEFT JOIN always duplicates rows > Check `GROUP BY key HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` on the side that should be unique. --- Which pattern finds customers who never placed an order, safely even with NULLs? - `WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)` * `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)` - `INNER JOIN orders ... WHERE order_id IS NULL` > NOT EXISTS ignores NULLs in the subquery. An inner join can never produce a NULL order_id. ```

title: Aggregation
md:
By the end of this chapter you can turn a million rows into the handful of numbers a business asks for, count several things in one pass, build subtotals, and explain why the average order value can mislead. ## GROUP BY in one picture GROUP BY collapses rows that share the same values into one row per group, and aggregate functions summarise each group: ```sql SELECT channel, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross, ROUND(AVG(quantity * unit_price)) AS avg_order_value FROM shop_orders GROUP BY channel ORDER BY gross DESC; ``` The rule: every column in SELECT is either in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate. Otherwise the engine doesn't know which of the many values to show. DuckDB, Databricks and Snowflake accept `GROUP BY ALL`, which groups by every non-aggregated column for you. ## The aggregate functions you'll use | Function | Returns | Watch out | |---|---|---| | `COUNT(*)` | rows | counts NULL rows too | | `COUNT(col)` | non-NULL values | | | `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` | distinct non-NULL values | expensive on big data: see below | | `SUM`, `AVG` | total, mean | ignore NULLs | | `MIN`, `MAX` | smallest, largest | work on dates and text too | | `MEDIAN`, `quantile_cont(col, 0.9)` | middle, 90th percentile | names differ by engine | | `STRING_AGG(col, ', ')` | values joined into text | `LISTAGG` in Snowflake, `collect_list` in Spark | ## Mean versus median ```sql SELECT ROUND(AVG(quantity * unit_price)) AS mean_order, quantile_cont(quantity * unit_price, 0.5) AS median_order, quantile_cont(quantity * unit_price, 0.9) AS p90_order FROM shop_orders; ``` The mean is about ₹37,000 but the median is about ₹21,000. A few very large orders pull the mean up. When someone asks for a "typical" order, give the median and say why. The same goes for latency, delivery time and salaries. ## Count many things in one pass A dashboard often needs several counts. Don't write five queries; use FILTER (DuckDB, Postgres, Spark 3.2+) or CASE inside the aggregate (works everywhere): ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'delivered') AS delivered, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled, SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'returned' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS returned, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') / COUNT(*), 2) AS cancel_rate_pct FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01'; ``` One scan of the table instead of five. On a warehouse that bills by data scanned, that's five times cheaper. ## HAVING filters groups ```sql SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross FROM shop_orders WHERE status = 'delivered' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20 ORDER BY gross DESC LIMIT 10; ``` WHERE removes cancelled orders before grouping; HAVING keeps only customers with 20 or more delivered orders after grouping. Put every condition you can in WHERE, because fewer rows reach the grouping step. ## Shares of a total "What share of revenue does each payment method bring?" needs the group total and the grand total together. A window over the grouped result does it in one query: ```sql SELECT payment_method, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(quantity * unit_price) / SUM(SUM(quantity * unit_price)) OVER (), 1) AS share_pct FROM shop_orders GROUP BY payment_method ORDER BY gross DESC; ``` `SUM(SUM(...)) OVER ()` looks strange: the inner SUM is the group total, the outer window SUM adds up all groups. Window functions get their own chapter (9). ## Subtotals with ROLLUP Finance reports want subtotals and a grand total. ROLLUP adds them: ```sql SELECT channel, payment_method, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM shop_orders GROUP BY ROLLUP (channel, payment_method) ORDER BY channel NULLS LAST, payment_method NULLS LAST; ``` Rows where payment_method is NULL are channel subtotals; the row where both are NULL is the grand total. `CUBE` gives subtotals for every combination, and `GROUPING SETS` lets you list exactly the ones you want. Use `GROUPING(col)` to tell a subtotal NULL from a real NULL. ## Pivoting rows into columns ```sql SELECT channel, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE payment_method = 'UPI') AS upi, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE payment_method = 'Card') AS card, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE payment_method = 'Cash on delivery') AS cod FROM shop_orders GROUP BY channel ORDER BY channel; ``` Conditional aggregation is the portable pivot. Many engines also have a `PIVOT` keyword, but its syntax differs everywhere (chapter 19). ## Counting distinct values at scale `COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)` has to remember every value it has seen, which is slow and memory-hungry on billions of rows. When an exact number isn't needed, use an approximate count: ```sql SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS exact_users, approx_count_distinct(user_id) AS approx_users FROM web_events; ``` The approximate version uses a HyperLogLog sketch. On this table it lands a few percent off the exact count but needs only a few kilobytes of memory however many values there are. Use it for dashboards and monitoring, never for billing or reconciliation. Spark, Databricks, BigQuery and Snowflake all have it under similar names. ## Common mistakes - **A column in SELECT that isn't grouped or aggregated.** Most engines refuse; MySQL used to pick a random value. - **AVG of an average.** The average of daily averages is not the overall average when days have different volumes. Sum and count separately, then divide. - **COUNT(*) after a join** that fanned out (chapter 5). - **Integer division in rates.** Multiply by `100.0`. - **Grouping by a timestamp** when you meant a day. Use `date_trunc('day', order_ts)` (chapter 10). ## In the interview **"WHERE or HAVING?"** WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after. Then mention the performance reason. **"How would you count orders per status in a single row?"** Conditional aggregation with FILTER or CASE, one scan. Practice 23 is this exact question. **"Why is your average different from finance's?"** Probably one of: NULL handling, cancelled orders included or not, or an average of averages. Asking which definition they use is the senior answer. ```quiz Daily average order values are ₹100 (10 orders) and ₹200 (90 orders). What is the overall average order value? - ₹150 * ₹190 - ₹200 > Total value is 10 × 100 + 90 × 200 = 19,000 over 100 orders. Averaging the two averages gives the wrong ₹150. --- Which query keeps only customers with at least 5 orders? - `... WHERE COUNT(*) >= 5 GROUP BY customer_id` * `... GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5` - `... GROUP BY customer_id WHERE COUNT(*) >= 5` > Aggregates can't go in WHERE, because groups don't exist yet when WHERE runs. --- After `GROUP BY ROLLUP (channel, payment_method)`, what does a row with channel = 'app' and payment_method NULL mean? - Orders from the app with no payment method recorded * The subtotal for all app orders - The grand total > ROLLUP adds a subtotal per channel and a grand total. Use GROUPING() to tell it from a real NULL. ```

title: Subqueries and CTEs
md:
By the end of this chapter you can break any hard question into small named steps, choose between a subquery, a CTE and a temp table, and walk a hierarchy with a recursive CTE. ## Why this matters Interview questions and real pipeline logic are rarely one SELECT. "Customers who spend more than the average customer in their city" is three steps: spend per customer, average per city, compare. CTEs let you write those steps in order, each with a name, so you and your reviewer can check each one. ## Subqueries: a query inside a query A subquery can stand wherever a value, a list or a table can: ```sql -- As a single value (scalar subquery) SELECT order_id, quantity * unit_price AS gross FROM shop_orders WHERE quantity * unit_price > (SELECT AVG(quantity * unit_price) * 5 FROM shop_orders) LIMIT 10; ``` ```sql -- As a list SELECT COUNT(*) AS premium_orders FROM shop_orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM shop_customers WHERE is_premium); ``` ```sql -- As a table (derived table) SELECT segment, ROUND(AVG(orders), 1) AS avg_orders_per_customer FROM ( SELECT c.segment, o.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM shop_orders o JOIN shop_customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.segment, o.customer_id ) per_customer GROUP BY segment ORDER BY segment; ``` A scalar subquery must return exactly one row and one column, or the query fails at run time. ## Correlated subqueries A correlated subquery refers to the outer row, so in principle it runs once per row: ```sql SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, (SELECT MAX(o.order_ts) FROM shop_orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS last_order_ts FROM shop_customers c WHERE c.city = 'Pune' LIMIT 10; ``` Modern optimisers usually rewrite this into a join, but not always. If a correlated subquery is slow, rewrite it as a join to a grouped CTE yourself. ## CTEs: name each step `WITH name AS (...)` defines a temporary named result that the rest of the query can use. Here is the city-average question, step by step: ```sql WITH spend AS ( SELECT o.customer_id, c.city, SUM(o.quantity * o.unit_price) AS gross FROM shop_orders o JOIN shop_customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY o.customer_id, c.city ), city_avg AS ( SELECT city, AVG(gross) AS avg_gross FROM spend GROUP BY city ) SELECT s.city, COUNT(*) AS above_avg_customers FROM spend s JOIN city_avg a ON a.city = s.city WHERE s.gross > a.avg_gross GROUP BY s.city ORDER BY above_avg_customers DESC LIMIT 5; ``` Read it top to bottom like a recipe. To debug, swap the final SELECT for `SELECT * FROM spend LIMIT 10` and check each step on its own. This is how dbt models are written too (handbook 11). ## Subquery, CTE or temp table? | Use | When | |---|---| | Subquery | a small, one-off piece used once | | CTE | several steps, or the same step used twice in one query | | Temp table | a heavy intermediate result reused by several queries, or one you want to inspect or index | | View | logic other people and jobs should reuse (chapter 15) | A CTE is mainly for readability. Some engines compute a CTE once and reuse it; others inline it each time it's referenced. If a CTE is expensive and referenced several times, check the plan or use a temp table. ## Recursive CTEs A recursive CTE has a starting query and a step that refers to itself, repeated until it adds no rows. Two everyday uses: generating sequences and walking hierarchies. ```sql -- Generate the 12 months of 2025 WITH RECURSIVE months(month) AS ( SELECT DATE '2025-01-01' UNION ALL SELECT CAST(month + INTERVAL 1 MONTH AS DATE) FROM months WHERE month < DATE '2025-12-01' ) SELECT month FROM months; ``` ```sql -- Walk a reporting line: everyone under manager 1, with their depth WITH RECURSIVE staff(emp_id, name, manager_id) AS ( VALUES (1, 'Asha', NULL), (2, 'Ravi', 1), (3, 'Meera', 1), (4, 'Kabir', 2), (5, 'Zoya', 4), (6, 'Dev', 3) ), tree AS ( SELECT emp_id, name, manager_id, 0 AS depth, name AS path FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT s.emp_id, s.name, s.manager_id, t.depth + 1, t.path || ' > ' || s.name FROM staff s JOIN tree t ON s.manager_id = t.emp_id ) SELECT depth, name, path FROM tree ORDER BY path; ``` Always make sure the recursive step can stop. A cycle in the data (A manages B, B manages A) loops forever unless you cap the depth with `WHERE t.depth < 20`. Spark SQL only gained recursive CTEs recently, so older Spark jobs walk hierarchies with a loop in Python instead. ## Common mistakes - **A scalar subquery that returns two rows.** Fails at run time, often only on production data. - **NOT IN with a nullable subquery.** Use NOT EXISTS (chapter 4). - **One giant query with five nested subqueries.** Split it into CTEs. - **Assuming a CTE is cached.** It may be recomputed each time it's used. - **A recursive CTE with no stop condition.** ## In the interview **"CTE vs subquery vs temp table?"** Readability and reuse within one query for a CTE, a one-off for a subquery, and a temp table when an expensive result is reused across queries or needs inspecting. Mention that CTE materialisation depends on the engine. **"Find all reports under a manager at any level."** A recursive CTE with an anchor (the manager) and a step joining employees to the rows found so far. Mention cycle protection. ```quiz A scalar subquery in SELECT returns two rows for one customer. What happens? - The engine picks the first row * The query fails with an error - The customer appears twice > A scalar subquery must return at most one row. Aggregate it, or turn it into a join. --- What makes a recursive CTE stop? - It always runs exactly 100 times * The recursive step returns no new rows - The engine detects the end of the table > Each pass feeds the previous pass's rows into the step. When the step adds nothing, it ends. Guard against cycles. --- You reference an expensive CTE three times in one query and it's slow. What is a good fix? - Rename the CTE * Materialise the result into a temp table, then query it - Add ORDER BY inside the CTE > Some engines recompute a CTE at each reference. A temp table computes it once. ```

title: Set operations
md:
By the end of this chapter you can stack, intersect and subtract result sets, you know why UNION ALL is the default in pipelines, and you can use EXCEPT to reconcile a source against a target. ## Stacking results Set operations combine whole result sets top to bottom, not side by side like a join. Both sides must have the same number of columns with compatible types, matched by position, not by name. | Operation | Returns | Removes duplicates? | |---|---|---| | `UNION ALL` | every row from both sides | no | | `UNION` | every distinct row from both sides | yes | | `INTERSECT` | rows that appear on both sides | yes | | `EXCEPT` (`MINUS` in Oracle and Snowflake) | rows on the left that are not on the right | yes | ## UNION ALL is the pipeline default ```sql SELECT 'web' AS source, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM shop_orders WHERE channel = 'web' UNION ALL SELECT 'app', COUNT(*) FROM shop_orders WHERE channel = 'app' UNION ALL SELECT 'marketplace', COUNT(*) FROM shop_orders WHERE channel = 'marketplace'; ``` `UNION` has to sort or hash every row to remove duplicates, which is expensive on big data, and it can quietly delete rows you meant to keep: two genuine ₹500 orders from the same customer on the same day look identical if you didn't select order_id. Use `UNION ALL` unless you truly want duplicates removed, and say why when you do. ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS union_all_rows FROM ( SELECT city FROM shop_customers WHERE country = 'India' UNION ALL SELECT city FROM shop_customers WHERE segment = 'Corporate' ); ``` ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS union_rows FROM ( SELECT city FROM shop_customers WHERE country = 'India' UNION SELECT city FROM shop_customers WHERE segment = 'Corporate' ); ``` The first counts every row from both sides. The second collapses them to the distinct list of cities. ## Matching columns by name Because columns match by position, a swapped column order puts emails in the name column without any error. DuckDB and Spark offer a safer form: ```sql SELECT customer_id, email FROM shop_customers WHERE customer_id <= 2 UNION ALL BY NAME SELECT email, customer_id FROM shop_customers WHERE customer_id BETWEEN 3 AND 4; ``` In Spark the DataFrame equivalent is `df1.unionByName(df2, allowMissingColumns=True)`, which you'll use when appending files whose schema changes over time. ## INTERSECT and EXCEPT ```sql -- Customers who paid by both UPI and card SELECT customer_id FROM shop_orders WHERE payment_method = 'UPI' INTERSECT SELECT customer_id FROM shop_orders WHERE payment_method = 'Card' LIMIT 10; ``` ```sql -- Customers who used UPI but never cash on delivery SELECT COUNT(*) AS upi_never_cod FROM ( SELECT customer_id FROM shop_orders WHERE payment_method = 'UPI' EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM shop_orders WHERE payment_method = 'Cash on delivery' ); ``` Unlike NOT IN, EXCEPT treats NULLs as equal to each other, so a NULL on both sides cancels out instead of breaking the result. ## Reconciling source and target After a load, data engineers check that the target matches the source. EXCEPT in both directions finds every difference: ```sql WITH source(id, city) AS ( VALUES (1, 'Pune'), (2, 'Mumbai'), (3, 'Delhi'), (4, NULL) ), target(id, city) AS ( VALUES (1, 'Pune'), (2, 'Bengaluru'), (4, NULL), (5, 'Goa') ) SELECT 'missing or changed in target' AS problem, * FROM (SELECT * FROM source EXCEPT SELECT * FROM target) UNION ALL SELECT 'extra or changed in target', * FROM (SELECT * FROM target EXCEPT SELECT * FROM source) ORDER BY id; ``` Id 2 shows on both sides because its city changed, id 3 never arrived, and id 5 shouldn't be there. Id 4 matches even though its city is NULL. On large tables you'd compare row counts and column checksums per partition first, and only run the full EXCEPT on partitions that disagree (chapter 18). ## Common mistakes - **UNION by habit.** Slower, and it can drop real rows. - **Columns in a different order** on each side. No error, wrong data. - **ORDER BY inside one branch.** It applies to the whole result, so put it once at the end. - **Mismatched types** like an integer id against a string id. Cast explicitly on both sides. ## In the interview **"UNION vs UNION ALL?"** UNION removes duplicates, so it sorts or hashes the whole result; UNION ALL just appends. Default to UNION ALL in pipelines, both for speed and because UNION can delete legitimate duplicate rows. **"How do you check a target table matches its source?"** Row counts first, then checksums per partition, then EXCEPT in both directions on the partitions that differ. ```quiz Branch A returns 10 rows and branch B returns 10 rows. 4 rows are identical across them and there are no duplicates within a branch. How many rows does UNION return? - 20 * 16 - 4 > UNION keeps each distinct row once: 10 + 10 − 4 = 16. UNION ALL would return 20. --- Why is UNION ALL usually preferred in pipelines? - It sorts the output * It doesn't deduplicate, so it's faster and never drops genuine duplicate rows - It matches columns by name > Deduplication needs a sort or hash of everything. Do it deliberately, on a key, when you need it. --- `SELECT name, email FROM a UNION ALL SELECT email, name FROM b` runs without error. What's wrong? - Nothing * Columns match by position, so emails land in the name column for b's rows - UNION ALL needs the same table on both sides > Name the columns in the same order, or use UNION ALL BY NAME where it's supported. ```

title: Window functions
md:
By the end of this chapter you can rank, number, compare and accumulate rows without losing detail, deduplicate with ROW_NUMBER, control window frames, and solve the gaps-and-islands questions that every DE interview loves. ## What a window function does GROUP BY collapses rows. A window function keeps every row and adds a value computed over a set of related rows, the "window". That's why it's the tool for "rank within", "previous value", "running total" and "latest per key". ```sql SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_ts, quantity * unit_price AS gross, SUM(quantity * unit_price) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_orders FROM shop_orders WHERE customer_id IN (101, 102) ORDER BY customer_id, order_ts LIMIT 12; ``` The anatomy: `function() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... frame)`. - **PARTITION BY** splits rows into groups, like GROUP BY but without collapsing. - **ORDER BY** sets the order inside each partition. - **The frame** picks which rows around the current one count (see below). ## Ranking: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK ```sql SELECT score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS row_number, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rank, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS dense_rank FROM (VALUES (100), (100), (90), (80)) t(score); ``` | Function | Ties | After a tie of two at 1st | |---|---|---| | `ROW_NUMBER` | always unique, ties broken arbitrarily | 1, 2, 3 | | `RANK` | ties share, then skips | 1, 1, 3 | | `DENSE_RANK` | ties share, no gaps | 1, 1, 2 | For "top 3 per group", decide what a tie should do before choosing. "Top 3 products by revenue in each category" with DENSE_RANK can return more than 3 rows when there are ties, and that's often what the business wants. ## Top N per group ```sql WITH product_sales AS ( SELECT p.category, p.product_name, SUM(o.quantity * o.unit_price) AS gross FROM shop_orders o JOIN shop_products p ON p.product_id = o.product_id WHERE o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY p.category, p.product_name ) SELECT category, product_name, gross, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY gross DESC) AS rnk FROM product_sales QUALIFY rnk <= 3 ORDER BY category, rnk; ``` `QUALIFY` filters on a window result, the way HAVING filters on an aggregate. It works in DuckDB, Databricks, Snowflake and BigQuery. In Postgres, SQL Server and older Spark, wrap the query and filter in the outer WHERE. ## Deduplicate: latest row per key This is the single most used window pattern in data engineering. Web events arrive twice sometimes; keep one per event_id: ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_before, COUNT(DISTINCT event_id) AS unique_events FROM web_events; ``` ```sql SELECT event_id, user_id, event_ts, event_type FROM web_events QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC) = 1 LIMIT 10; ``` The same shape keeps the latest version of each customer in a CDC feed: partition by the business key, order by the update timestamp descending, keep row 1. Always add a tie-breaker to the ORDER BY (an ingestion id or file name). With a tie, ROW_NUMBER picks arbitrarily and the "latest" row can change between runs. ## LAG and LEAD: compare with neighbours ```sql WITH daily AS ( SELECT CAST(order_ts AS DATE) AS day, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS revenue FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-03-01' AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-03-15' GROUP BY day ) SELECT day, revenue, LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS prev_day, revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS change, ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day)) / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day), 1) AS change_pct FROM daily ORDER BY day; ``` `LAG(col, n, default)` looks n rows back; `LEAD` looks forward. The first row has no previous one, so LAG returns NULL unless you give a default. ```sql -- Days between a customer's consecutive orders SELECT customer_id, order_ts, DATE_DIFF('day', LAG(order_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts), order_ts) AS days_since_prev FROM shop_orders WHERE customer_id = 101 ORDER BY order_ts LIMIT 10; ``` ## Running totals and moving averages: frames With an ORDER BY, aggregate windows become cumulative. The frame says exactly which rows count: ```sql WITH daily AS ( SELECT CAST(order_ts AS DATE) AS day, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01' AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-02-01' GROUP BY day ) SELECT day, orders, SUM(orders) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total, ROUND(AVG(orders) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS moving_avg_7d, SUM(orders) OVER (PARTITION BY date_trunc('week', day) ORDER BY day) AS week_to_date FROM daily ORDER BY day; ``` **ROWS vs RANGE.** `ROWS` counts physical rows. `RANGE` groups rows with equal ORDER BY values. The default frame when you write ORDER BY without a frame is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, so tied rows all get the same running total, which surprises people: ```sql SELECT day, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS default_range, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rows_frame FROM (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20), (2, 30), (3, 40)) t(day, amount); ``` Write the frame explicitly whenever you mean ROWS. A 7-day moving average over ROWS is only correct if every day has a row, so fill missing days first (chapter 5's cross join, or chapter 10). ## FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTILE ```sql SELECT customer_id, quantity * unit_price AS gross, FIRST_VALUE(quantity * unit_price) OVER w AS first_order_value, LAST_VALUE(quantity * unit_price) OVER (w ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_order_value FROM shop_orders WHERE customer_id = 101 WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts) ORDER BY order_ts LIMIT 5; ``` LAST_VALUE with the default frame only sees up to the current row, so it just returns the current row. Give it the full frame, as above. `NTILE(4)` splits rows into four nearly equal buckets: quartiles of customer spend in practice 36. ## Gaps and islands "Users who were active 3 or more days in a row" is the classic. The trick: for consecutive dates, `date - ROW_NUMBER()` is constant, so it labels each streak. ```sql WITH days AS ( SELECT DISTINCT user_id, CAST(event_ts AS DATE) AS day FROM web_events WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL AND user_id <= 200 ), grouped AS ( SELECT user_id, day, day - CAST(ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day) AS INTEGER) AS streak_id FROM days ) SELECT user_id, MIN(day) AS streak_start, MAX(day) AS streak_end, COUNT(*) AS days FROM grouped GROUP BY user_id, streak_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 ORDER BY days DESC, user_id LIMIT 10; ``` The same idea collapses consecutive numbers into ranges (practice 49) and finds the longest streak (practice 42). The other gaps-and-islands tool is "flag a change with LAG, then running-sum the flags", which builds sessions from clicks (practice 47). ## Performance notes - Every distinct `PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY` needs its own sort. Reuse one window definition with `WINDOW w AS (...)` when you can. - A window with no PARTITION BY puts every row into one partition. In Spark that means one task processes the whole table, and you'll see the warning "No Partition Defined for Window operation". Partition by something whenever the question allows it. - Filtering before the window (in WHERE) is cheaper than filtering after (in QUALIFY). ## Common mistakes - **ROW_NUMBER without a tie-breaker** in dedup logic. Results change between runs. - **Filtering a window result in WHERE.** Use QUALIFY or an outer query. - **LAST_VALUE with the default frame.** - **Moving averages over ROWS with missing days.** - **Expecting a window to collapse rows.** Add DISTINCT or group afterwards if you need one row per partition. ## In the interview **"ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK on 100, 100, 90?"** 1, 2, 3; 1, 1, 3; 1, 1, 2. Then say which you'd use for "top 3 salaries per department" and why ties matter. **"Remove duplicates, keep the latest."** ROW_NUMBER over the key, ordered by timestamp descending with a tie-breaker, keep 1. Mention QUALIFY and that this is how you'd dedup a CDC feed before a MERGE. **"Users who logged in 3 days in a row."** The date minus ROW_NUMBER trick. Explain why it works, not just the code. ```quiz Scores are 100, 100 and 90. What does DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) return? - 1, 2, 3 - 1, 1, 3 * 1, 1, 2 > DENSE_RANK shares ranks on ties and leaves no gap. RANK would give 1, 1, 3. --- `SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY day)` gives two rows with the same day the same running total. Why? - It's a bug in the engine * The default frame is RANGE, which treats rows with equal ORDER BY values as one step - SUM ignores duplicates > Write `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` to count physical rows one by one. --- Why does `date - ROW_NUMBER()` find streaks of consecutive days? - ROW_NUMBER skips missing days * Within a streak both rise by 1 each row, so the difference stays the same and labels the streak - It only works on weekdays > When a day is missing, the date jumps by more than the row number does, so the difference changes and a new streak starts. ```

title: Dates and times
md:
By the end of this chapter you can bucket timestamps into days, weeks and months, do date arithmetic, fill missing dates, build retention and churn numbers, and avoid the time zone and boundary bugs that make daily numbers disagree. ## Dates are where pipelines break Most pipelines run on a time window: "load yesterday", "rebuild last month". A wrong boundary double counts or drops a day, and a time zone mix-up shifts revenue across midnight. Get these few patterns right and most date bugs disappear. ## Types | Type | Holds | Example | |---|---|---| | `DATE` | a calendar day | `DATE '2025-03-14'` | | `TIMESTAMP` | date and time, no zone | `TIMESTAMP '2025-03-14 18:30:00'` | | `TIMESTAMPTZ` / `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` | an instant in time | stored in UTC, shown in the session zone | | `INTERVAL` | a duration | `INTERVAL 7 DAY` | Store event times in UTC and convert to a local zone (India is UTC+5:30) only for reporting. When a source sends local time with no zone, write down which zone it is in the pipeline's docs: you can't recover it later. ## Truncate and extract ```sql SELECT order_ts, CAST(order_ts AS DATE) AS day, date_trunc('week', order_ts) AS week_start, date_trunc('month', order_ts) AS month_start, EXTRACT(year FROM order_ts) AS yr, EXTRACT(quarter FROM order_ts) AS qtr, dayname(order_ts) AS weekday, EXTRACT(hour FROM order_ts) AS hr FROM shop_orders LIMIT 5; ``` `date_trunc` keeps a timestamp you can sort and join on; `EXTRACT` gives a number. For monthly reports, group by `date_trunc('month', ...)`, not by `EXTRACT(month ...)`, or January 2024 and January 2025 land in the same bucket. ```sql SELECT date_trunc('month', order_ts) AS month, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross FROM shop_orders GROUP BY month ORDER BY month; ``` Weeks start on Monday in DuckDB, Spark and Postgres (ISO weeks), but on Sunday in some BI tools. Agree on one with the business. ## Arithmetic ```sql SELECT DATE '2025-01-31' + INTERVAL 1 MONTH AS plus_month, DATE '2025-03-14' - INTERVAL 7 DAY AS minus_week, DATE '2025-03-14' - DATE '2025-01-01' AS days_between, DATE_DIFF('day', DATE '2025-01-01', DATE '2025-03-14') AS diff_days, DATE_DIFF('month', DATE '2025-01-31', DATE '2025-02-01') AS diff_months, last_day(DATE '2024-02-10') AS month_end; ``` Two surprises worth remembering. Adding one month to 31 January gives 28 February, because there is no 31st. And `DATE_DIFF('month', ...)` counts month boundaries crossed, so 31 January to 1 February is one month. Function names differ by engine: `datediff`, `date_add` and `add_months` in Spark (chapter 19 has the full table). ## Windows of time: always half-open ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders_last_7_days FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-12-31' - INTERVAL 7 DAY AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-12-31'; ``` Start inclusive, end exclusive, as in chapter 3. In a real job the end comes from the scheduler's run date, not `CURRENT_DATE`, so rerunning last Tuesday's job reloads last Tuesday's window and nothing else. That's what makes a job safe to backfill (handbook 10, Airflow). ## Fill missing dates A chart of daily sales must show zero on days with no sales, not skip them. Generate every day, then left join: ```sql WITH days AS ( SELECT CAST(d AS DATE) AS day FROM generate_series(TIMESTAMP '2025-02-01', TIMESTAMP '2025-02-28', INTERVAL 1 DAY) t(d) ), cod AS ( SELECT CAST(order_ts AS DATE) AS day, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM shop_orders WHERE payment_method = 'Cash on delivery' AND channel = 'marketplace' AND quantity = 6 AND order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-02-01' AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-03-01' GROUP BY day ) SELECT d.day, COALESCE(c.orders, 0) AS orders FROM days d LEFT JOIN cod c ON c.day = d.day ORDER BY d.day; ``` In Spark use `sequence(start, end, interval 1 day)` with `explode`. Many warehouses keep a permanent calendar table with one row per day plus holiday and fiscal-period columns, which is better than generating one each time (chapter 14). ## Cohorts, retention and churn Retention asks: of the people active in one period, how many came back in the next? Build one row per user per month, then join each month to the next: ```sql WITH active AS ( SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, date_trunc('month', order_ts) AS month FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01' ) SELECT a.month, COUNT(*) AS active_customers, COUNT(n.customer_id) AS retained_next_month, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(n.customer_id) / COUNT(*), 1) AS retention_pct FROM active a LEFT JOIN active n ON n.customer_id = a.customer_id AND n.month = a.month + INTERVAL 1 MONTH GROUP BY a.month ORDER BY a.month; ``` Customers active this month but not next are the churned ones; flip the join to an anti join to list them. Signup cohorts work the same way with the first order month as the starting point. Handbook 13 builds the full growth-accounting picture (new, retained, resurrected, churned) on top of this. ## Durations and overlaps ```sql SELECT trip_id, pickup_ts, dropoff_ts, DATE_DIFF('minute', pickup_ts, dropoff_ts) AS minutes FROM taxi_trips WHERE dropoff_ts <= pickup_ts OR DATE_DIFF('minute', pickup_ts, dropoff_ts) > 300 LIMIT 10; ``` A quality check like this catches trips that end before they start or last five hours. Two intervals overlap when `a.start < b.end AND b.start < a.end`, the condition behind practice 48 (overlapping bookings). ## Common mistakes - **BETWEEN on timestamps.** Drops most of the last day. - **Grouping by month number** across years. - **CURRENT_DATE inside a pipeline.** Reruns and backfills load the wrong window. Use the run date. - **Mixing UTC and local time** in one table. Daily totals shift by five and a half hours. - **Casting a string date without a format.** Is `03/04/2025` 3 April or 4 March? Use `strptime(s, '%d/%m/%Y')` (Spark: `to_date(s, 'dd/MM/yyyy')`). ## In the interview **"Month-over-month retention."** One row per user per month, join each month to the next on user, divide. Say how you treat a user who skips a month and returns: that's "resurrected", not retained. **"How do you make a daily job safe to rerun?"** A half-open window driven by the run date, and an overwrite of exactly that partition. No CURRENT_DATE. ```quiz You group 2024 and 2025 orders by `EXTRACT(month FROM order_ts)`. What goes wrong? - Nothing * January 2024 and January 2025 are added together - The query fails on leap years > Group by `date_trunc('month', order_ts)`, which keeps the year. --- Why shouldn't a daily pipeline filter with `CURRENT_DATE - 1`? - CURRENT_DATE is slow * A rerun or backfill for an old date loads the wrong day - It doesn't work in Spark > Drive the window from the scheduler's run date so every run is repeatable. --- When do intervals [a_start, a_end) and [b_start, b_end) overlap? - a_start = b_start * a_start < b_end AND b_start < a_end - a_end > b_end > Each must start before the other ends. This covers every overlap shape. ```

title: String functions and cleaning
md:
By the end of this chapter you can clean messy text into joinable keys, parse values out of strings with patterns, and standardise categories, which is most of what a silver layer does to text columns. ## Why text needs cleaning Sources are typed by people and stitched together by systems. The same city arrives as `Bengaluru`, ` bengaluru `, `BENGALURU` and `Bangalore`. Joins on uncleaned text silently miss rows, and group-bys split one city into four. Cleaning text into a standard form is one of the first jobs of the silver layer. ## The everyday functions ```sql SELECT full_name, upper(full_name) AS up, lower(email) AS email_lower, length(full_name) AS len, split_part(email, '@', 1) AS local_part, split_part(email, '@', 2) AS domain, left(full_name, 3) AS first3, full_name || ' (' || city || ')' AS label, concat_ws(', ', full_name, city, country) AS label_skip_nulls FROM shop_customers LIMIT 5; ``` Note the last two. `||` returns NULL if any part is NULL, so a customer with no city gets a NULL label. `concat_ws` skips NULLs. In Spark, `concat` behaves like `||` and `concat_ws` skips NULLs too. ## Clean a messy column ```sql WITH raw(city_raw) AS ( VALUES (' Bengaluru'), ('bengaluru '), ('BENGALURU'), ('Bangalore'), ('Mumbai'), ('mumbai'), ('Bombay'), (''), (NULL), ('N/A') ) SELECT city_raw, CASE WHEN NULLIF(trim(city_raw), '') IS NULL THEN NULL WHEN upper(trim(city_raw)) IN ('N/A', 'NA', '-') THEN NULL WHEN lower(trim(city_raw)) = 'bangalore' THEN 'Bengaluru' WHEN lower(trim(city_raw)) = 'bombay' THEN 'Mumbai' ELSE upper(left(trim(city_raw), 1)) || lower(substr(trim(city_raw), 2)) END AS city_clean FROM raw; ``` DuckDB has no `initcap`, so the last line capitalises by hand; Spark, Postgres and Snowflake have `initcap`. The order matters: trim first, turn empty strings and placeholders like `N/A` into real NULLs, map known aliases, then standardise the case. In a real pipeline the alias list lives in a small mapping table you join to, so analysts can add `Gurgaon → Gurugram` without a code change. ## Pattern matching ```sql SELECT email, email LIKE '%@example.com' AS like_match, regexp_matches(email, '^[a-z]+\.[0-9]+@') AS regex_match, regexp_extract(email, '\.([0-9]+)@', 1) AS number_in_email, regexp_replace(full_name, '[aeiou]', '*', 'g') AS masked FROM shop_customers LIMIT 5; ``` | Tool | Use for | |---|---| | `LIKE` / `ILIKE` | simple prefix, suffix or contains checks, fast | | `regexp_matches` (`RLIKE` in Spark) | validating a format | | `regexp_extract` | pulling a part out of a string | | `regexp_replace` | removing or masking characters | Regex is powerful but slow on billions of rows and hard to review. Use LIKE when it's enough and comment every regex. ## Validate before you trust ```sql WITH phones(raw) AS ( VALUES ('+91 98765 43210'), ('098765-43210'), ('9876543210'), ('12345'), ('call me') ) SELECT raw, regexp_replace(raw, '[^0-9]', '', 'g') AS digits, right(regexp_replace(raw, '[^0-9]', '', 'g'), 10) AS last10, length(regexp_replace(raw, '[^0-9]', '', 'g')) >= 10 AS looks_valid FROM phones; ``` Strip to digits, keep a standard length, and flag what doesn't fit instead of guessing. Bad rows go to a quarantine table with a reason, not into silver (chapter 18). ## Keys and hashing Text keys are often normalised before joining or hashing: ```sql SELECT email, md5(lower(trim(email))) AS email_key, hash(lower(trim(email))) AS email_hash64 FROM shop_customers WHERE email IS NOT NULL LIMIT 5; ``` Hashing a normalised value gives a stable key for joins and deduplication across systems. A hash also hides the raw email in shared tables, though a plain MD5 of an email can be reversed by guessing, so treat it as pseudonymous, not anonymous. Spark has `md5`, `sha2(col, 256)` and `xxhash64`. ## Common mistakes - **Joining on raw text** with stray spaces or mixed case. - **Empty string versus NULL.** They are different values; `COUNT(col)` counts empty strings. Convert one to the other early and consistently. - **`||` with a nullable column.** The whole result becomes NULL. - **Collation surprises.** Some warehouses compare case-insensitively by default and others don't. Don't depend on it; normalise. - **Unicode.** `Müller` and `Muller` don't match, and some lengths count bytes rather than characters. Test with real names. ## In the interview **"Find duplicate emails."** Group by `lower(trim(email))` having count > 1, and say that you normalised first, because `A@x.com` and `a@x.com ` are the same person. That one sentence shows you've cleaned real data. **"How would you standardise city names from five sources?"** Trim, normalise case, map aliases through a maintained mapping table, send unknowns to a review queue, and track the unmapped rate as a quality metric. ```quiz `SELECT 'Asha' || NULL` returns what? - 'Asha' * NULL - An error > `||` propagates NULL. Use concat_ws or COALESCE when parts can be missing. --- Which step should come first when cleaning a city column? * Trim spaces and turn empty strings and placeholders into NULL - Map aliases like Bombay to Mumbai - Group by city > Alias matching only works on trimmed, normalised text. --- Is an MD5 hash of an email address anonymous? - Yes, MD5 can't be reversed * No, someone can hash likely emails and compare, so it's only pseudonymous - Only if it's uppercase > Use a secret salt or a keyed hash if the data must not be re-identified. ```

title: Semi-structured data: JSON, arrays and structs
md:
By the end of this chapter you can query nested data with arrays and structs, explode a list into rows and roll rows back into a list, and pull fields out of raw JSON the way bronze-to-silver jobs do. ## Why DEs meet nested data daily APIs return JSON. Kafka messages are JSON or Avro. Event trackers send a payload whose fields change every sprint. Modern engines (Spark, Databricks, Snowflake, BigQuery, DuckDB) store this as nested columns instead of forcing it flat, so you need to read and reshape it with SQL. ## Arrays (lists) An array is an ordered list of values in one column: ```sql SELECT [10, 20, 30] AS arr, len([10, 20, 30]) AS n, [10, 20, 30][1] AS first_item, list_contains([10, 20, 30], 20) AS has_20, list_sort([3, 1, 2]) AS sorted; ``` Array indexes start at 1 in DuckDB, Snowflake's SQL functions vary, and Spark's `element_at` starts at 1 while `arr[0]` starts at 0. Check before you index. ## Explode: one row per item ```sql WITH baskets(order_id, items) AS ( VALUES (1, ['tea', 'biscuits']), (2, ['coffee']), (3, []) ) SELECT order_id, unnest(items) AS item FROM baskets; ``` Order 3 disappears because its list is empty, just like `explode` in Spark. Spark's `explode_outer` keeps it with a NULL item. Decide whether an empty basket should stay before you choose. ## Collect: many rows into one list ```sql SELECT customer_id, list(DISTINCT payment_method ORDER BY payment_method) AS methods_used, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM shop_orders WHERE customer_id BETWEEN 101 AND 105 GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id; ``` Spark calls these `collect_list` and `collect_set`; Snowflake uses `ARRAY_AGG`. This is how you build a "cumulative table" that keeps a user's whole history in one row, a pattern handbook 13 uses for fast activity reports. ## Structs: named fields in one column ```sql WITH people AS ( SELECT {'name': 'Asha', 'address': {'city': 'Pune', 'pin': '411001'}} AS person ) SELECT person.name, person.address.city, person.address.pin FROM people; ``` A struct is like a mini row inside a column. Dot notation reaches into it, at any depth. An array of structs, such as `[{'sku': 'A1', 'qty': 2}, ...]`, is the most common shape in order and event payloads: ```sql WITH orders(order_id, lines) AS ( VALUES (1, [{'sku': 'TEA-1', 'qty': 2}, {'sku': 'BIS-4', 'qty': 1}]), (2, [{'sku': 'COF-2', 'qty': 3}]) ) SELECT order_id, line.sku, line.qty FROM (SELECT order_id, unnest(lines) AS line FROM orders); ``` ## Raw JSON strings Bronze tables often keep the payload as a JSON string. You pull out the fields you need into typed columns in silver. In DuckDB: ```sql norun SELECT payload ->> '$.user.id' AS user_id, CAST(payload ->> '$.amount' AS DOUBLE) AS amount, payload -> '$.items' AS items_json, json_array_length(payload -> '$.items') AS item_count FROM raw_events; ``` The same in other engines: | Engine | Get a field as text | Parse to typed columns | |---|---|---| | DuckDB | `payload ->> '$.user.id'` | `from_json(payload, '{"user":{"id":"INTEGER"}}')` | | Spark / Databricks | `get_json_object(payload, '$.user.id')` or `payload:user.id` | `from_json(payload, schema)` | | Snowflake | `payload:user.id::int` on a VARIANT | `PARSE_JSON` then path access | | BigQuery | `JSON_VALUE(payload, '$.user.id')` | `JSON_EXTRACT_ARRAY` | | Postgres | `payload ->> 'user'` on JSONB | `jsonb_to_record` | Parse once into a typed schema in silver. Don't make every analyst re-parse JSON in every query: it's slow, and each person handles a missing field differently. ## Schema drift Payload fields appear, disappear and change type. Defensive habits: - Keep the raw payload in bronze, untouched, so you can re-parse later. - Parse with an explicit schema, not schema inference, so a surprise field doesn't change your table. - Route rows that fail to parse into a quarantine column or table (Databricks Auto Loader calls it `_rescued_data`). - Alert when a new field appears, then decide whether to add it. The Spark and Databricks handbooks show these with real files. ## Common mistakes - **Exploding before filtering.** Explode multiplies rows; filter the parent rows first. - **`explode` dropping empty or NULL arrays** when the business needed those rows. - **Leaving JSON as strings in silver.** Every query pays the parsing cost. - **Off-by-one array indexes** between engines. - **Schema inference in production.** One odd file changes the column types. ## In the interview **"Explode an array column into rows."** `unnest` or `explode`, and immediately mention empty arrays and `explode_outer`. Practice 68 is this one. **"How do you handle JSON whose schema changes?"** Raw in bronze, explicit schema in silver, quarantine for failures, an alert on new fields, and a reprocess path from bronze. ```quiz `explode` runs on an order whose items array is empty. What happens to that order? - It appears once with a NULL item * It disappears from the output - The query fails > Use explode_outer (Spark) or a LEFT JOIN on unnest to keep it. --- Where should raw JSON be parsed into typed columns? - In every analyst's query * Once, in the silver layer, with an explicit schema - In the source system > Bronze keeps the raw payload so you can reparse; silver holds clean typed columns. --- Which function rolls many rows into one list per group in Spark? - explode * collect_list - split > collect_list keeps duplicates; collect_set removes them. DuckDB calls it list(). ```
