title: Loading data: DML and pipeline patterns
md:
By the end of this chapter you can write the four load patterns every pipeline uses (full refresh, append, upsert, delete-and-insert), make a load safe to rerun, and load only what changed since last time. ## The DML statements ```sql CREATE TABLE stage_customers AS SELECT customer_id, full_name, city, segment FROM shop_customers WHERE customer_id <= 5; INSERT INTO stage_customers VALUES (100001, 'New Person', 'Goa', 'Consumer'); UPDATE stage_customers SET city = 'Pune' WHERE customer_id = 1; DELETE FROM stage_customers WHERE customer_id = 2; SELECT * FROM stage_customers ORDER BY customer_id; ``` | Statement | Removes | Can roll back? | Speed on big tables | |---|---|---|---| | `DELETE FROM t WHERE ...` | chosen rows | yes | slow: row by row, logged | | `TRUNCATE TABLE t` | all rows, keeps the table | depends on engine | fast | | `DROP TABLE t` | the table and its definition | depends on engine | fast | On a lakehouse table (Delta, Iceberg), DELETE and UPDATE rewrite the affected files. That's why partitioning and file layout matter for load speed (chapter 17). ## Pattern 1: full refresh Rebuild the whole table every run: ```sql CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dim_product AS SELECT product_id, product_name, category, brand, list_price FROM shop_products; SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_loaded FROM dim_product; ``` Simple and always correct, because it can't drift from the source. Use it for small dimensions and anything under a few million rows. It stops scaling when the source is large or keeps history the source no longer has. ## Pattern 2: append Add new rows, never change old ones. Right for immutable events like clicks and payments. The danger is running the same batch twice. Make appends safe with a check on a batch or event key: ```sql CREATE TABLE fact_events AS SELECT * FROM web_events WHERE event_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-01-02'; -- A batch that overlaps what we already loaded INSERT INTO fact_events SELECT n.* FROM web_events n WHERE n.event_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 12:00:00' AND n.event_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-01-03' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fact_events f WHERE f.event_id = n.event_id); SELECT COUNT(*) AS loaded, COUNT(DISTINCT event_id) AS unique_events FROM fact_events; ``` The overlap between the two batches didn't create new duplicates. The source itself has duplicate event_ids, which is why the two counts still differ: dedupe the batch with ROW_NUMBER (chapter 9) before inserting. ## Pattern 3: upsert with MERGE Update rows that exist, insert rows that don't. This is SCD Type 1 and the standard way to apply a CDC feed: ```sql CREATE TABLE dim_customer AS SELECT customer_id, full_name, city FROM shop_customers WHERE customer_id <= 3; CREATE TABLE changes(customer_id INTEGER, full_name VARCHAR, city VARCHAR); INSERT INTO changes VALUES (1, 'Zoya Singh', 'Nagpur'), (4, 'Brand New', 'Goa'); MERGE INTO dim_customer t USING changes s ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id WHEN MATCHED AND t.city IS DISTINCT FROM s.city THEN UPDATE SET city = s.city WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (customer_id, full_name, city) VALUES (s.customer_id, s.full_name, s.city); SELECT * FROM dim_customer ORDER BY customer_id; ``` Three things make a MERGE production-safe: 1. **The source has one row per key.** If `changes` had two rows for customer 1, MERGE fails or picks one at random. Dedupe first with ROW_NUMBER. 2. **The match condition uses `IS DISTINCT FROM`**, so NULL-to-value changes aren't missed (chapter 4), and unchanged rows aren't rewritten. 3. **Deletes are explicit.** If the CDC feed has an `op = 'D'` flag, add `WHEN MATCHED AND s.op = 'D' THEN DELETE`. Engines without MERGE use `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE` (Postgres, DuckDB) or an UPDATE followed by an INSERT of the missing keys. ```sql CREATE TABLE kv(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, val VARCHAR); INSERT INTO kv VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b'); INSERT INTO kv VALUES (2, 'B'), (3, 'c') ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET val = excluded.val; SELECT * FROM kv ORDER BY id; ``` ## Pattern 4: delete and insert a partition For daily facts, the simplest safe rerun is to replace exactly the slice you're loading: ```sql CREATE TABLE fact_daily_sales AS SELECT CAST(order_ts AS DATE) AS day, channel, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-01' AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-06-03' GROUP BY ALL; BEGIN; DELETE FROM fact_daily_sales WHERE day = DATE '2025-06-02'; INSERT INTO fact_daily_sales SELECT CAST(order_ts AS DATE), channel, SUM(quantity * unit_price) FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-02' AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-06-03' GROUP BY ALL; COMMIT; SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS channels, SUM(gross) AS gross FROM fact_daily_sales GROUP BY day ORDER BY day; ``` Run it twice and the table looks the same. That property, called idempotency, is the most important thing about any load. In Spark and Delta the same idea is `INSERT OVERWRITE ... PARTITION (day = ...)` or `replaceWhere`. ## Loading only what changed Reading the whole source every run gets expensive. Incremental loads keep a **watermark**: the highest change timestamp already loaded. ```sql CREATE TABLE load_state(table_name VARCHAR, last_loaded_ts TIMESTAMP); INSERT INTO load_state VALUES ('orders', TIMESTAMP '2025-12-30 00:00:00'); SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_to_load FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts > (SELECT last_loaded_ts FROM load_state WHERE table_name = 'orders') AND order_ts <= TIMESTAMP '2025-12-31 00:00:00'; UPDATE load_state SET last_loaded_ts = TIMESTAMP '2025-12-31 00:00:00' WHERE table_name = 'orders'; SELECT * FROM load_state; ``` The rules that keep a watermark honest: - Use a column that changes whenever the row changes (`updated_at`), not one set only on insert. - Set the upper bound at the start of the run and use it as the next watermark, so rows written during the run aren't skipped. - Move the watermark only after the load commits. - Late-arriving rows with old timestamps are missed. Re-read a small overlap (for example, the last two hours) and rely on MERGE to absorb repeats. - Watermarks can't see deletes. For those you need CDC from the database log (handbook 9) or a periodic full compare (chapter 8). ## Common mistakes - **Plain INSERT in a job that can be retried.** Every retry duplicates data. - **MERGE from a source with duplicate keys.** - **Moving the watermark before the load commits.** A failure loses that window for good. - **`WHERE updated_at > watermark` with `=` rows at the boundary** being skipped or doubled. Pick `>` or `>=` deliberately and dedupe. - **DELETE without WHERE.** Run the WHERE as a SELECT first. ## In the interview **"How do you make a pipeline idempotent?"** Replace a well-defined slice (delete and insert, or overwrite a partition), or MERGE on a unique key from a deduplicated source. Running it twice must give the same table. **"Full load or incremental?"** Full while it's cheap, because it's simpler and self-healing. Incremental when volume or cost forces it, with a watermark, an overlap window, MERGE, and a periodic full reconcile. **"DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP?"** Chosen rows and logged; all rows, fast; the whole table and its definition. ```quiz A daily job inserts yesterday's orders with a plain INSERT. Airflow retries it after a timeout. What happens? - Nothing, the database ignores repeats * Yesterday's orders are loaded twice - The second run fails > Make it idempotent: delete and insert the day's partition, or MERGE on order_id. --- Your MERGE source has two rows for customer 7. What should you do? - Nothing, MERGE takes the newest * Deduplicate the source first, keeping the latest row per key - Switch to INSERT > Most engines fail or behave unpredictably on duplicate source keys. --- When should a pipeline move its watermark forward? - At the start of the run * After the load has committed successfully - Before reading the source > If the load fails after the watermark moved, that window is never loaded. ```
Practise thisSQL 60Upsert new and changed rows into a target (SCD Type 1)SQL 61SCD Type 2: keep history when a customer's city changesSQL 62Incremental load: only rows changed since the last loadSQL 63Rows in source missing from target, and rows that changedSQL 65Check staging for duplicate primary keys before loadingSQL 6Delete duplicates, keep the row with the smallest idSQL 12Swap 'M' and 'F' in one UPDATESQL 76DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP

title: Data modeling for analytics
md:
By the end of this chapter you can design a star schema from raw tables, choose a fact table's grain, build a date dimension, and keep history with SCD Type 2. Handbook 13 goes deeper into modeling patterns; this chapter gives you the SQL. ## Why model at all? Source tables are designed for the app that writes them: normalised, full of codes, changed often. Analysts need tables that are easy to query, fast and stable. Dimensional modeling (Kimball's star schema) is still the most common answer, on warehouses and lakehouses alike. ## Facts and dimensions - A **fact** table records events or measurements: one row per order line, payment or click. It holds foreign keys and numbers you add up. - A **dimension** table describes the things involved: customer, product, date, store. It holds the attributes you filter and group by. In a star schema, the fact sits in the middle and each dimension joins to it on one key. A snowflake schema splits dimensions further (product into category into department). Prefer the star: fewer joins, easier for people and BI tools. ## Step 1: choose the grain The grain is what one row of the fact means, stated in one sentence. "One row per order" and "one row per customer per day" are different tables. Decide it first; every other decision follows. Mixing grains, like daily totals in the same table as individual orders, is the most damaging modeling mistake because every SUM double counts. ## Step 2: build the dimensions ```sql CREATE TABLE dim_customer AS SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY customer_id) AS customer_sk, customer_id, full_name, COALESCE(city, 'Unknown') AS city, country, segment, is_premium, signup_date FROM shop_customers; SELECT * FROM dim_customer LIMIT 5; ``` `customer_sk` is a **surrogate key**: a number the warehouse owns, separate from the source's `customer_id` (the natural or business key). Surrogate keys let you keep several versions of the same customer (SCD Type 2 below) and survive a source system changing its ids. A **date dimension** saves every analyst from writing date logic: ```sql CREATE TABLE dim_date AS SELECT CAST(strftime(d, '%Y%m%d') AS INTEGER) AS date_key, CAST(d AS DATE) AS full_date, EXTRACT(year FROM d) AS year, EXTRACT(quarter FROM d) AS quarter, EXTRACT(month FROM d) AS month, monthname(d) AS month_name, dayname(d) AS day_name, EXTRACT(isodow FROM d) IN (6, 7) AS is_weekend, CASE WHEN EXTRACT(month FROM d) >= 4 THEN EXTRACT(year FROM d) ELSE EXTRACT(year FROM d) - 1 END AS fiscal_year_start FROM generate_series(TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01', TIMESTAMP '2025-12-31', INTERVAL 1 DAY) t(d); SELECT * FROM dim_date WHERE full_date BETWEEN DATE '2025-03-29' AND DATE '2025-04-02'; ``` The fiscal year column follows India's April-to-March year. Add holidays and sale events as columns too, and every report can use them. ## Step 3: build the fact ```sql CREATE TABLE dim_customer AS SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY customer_id) AS customer_sk, customer_id, city, segment FROM shop_customers; CREATE TABLE fact_orders AS SELECT o.order_id, CAST(strftime(o.order_ts, '%Y%m%d') AS INTEGER) AS date_key, c.customer_sk, o.product_id, o.channel, o.status, o.quantity, o.quantity * o.unit_price AS gross_amount, o.quantity * o.unit_price * o.discount_pct / 100.0 AS discount_amount FROM shop_orders o JOIN dim_customer c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-12-01'; SELECT c.segment, f.channel, SUM(f.gross_amount) AS gross FROM fact_orders f JOIN dim_customer c ON c.customer_sk = f.customer_sk GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY gross DESC; ``` Measures come in three kinds. **Additive** ones (amount, quantity) can be summed across every dimension. **Semi-additive** ones (an account balance) can be summed across customers but not across days. **Non-additive** ones (a ratio or a percentage) must be recomputed from their parts, never summed. ## Slowly changing dimensions Customers move cities. What should last year's report show? | Type | What happens on change | Use when | |---|---|---| | Type 0 | never change | fixed facts like date of birth | | Type 1 | overwrite | corrections, or history doesn't matter | | Type 2 | close the old row, add a new one | history matters: "sales by the city they lived in then" | | Type 3 | keep a "previous value" column | only the last change matters | Type 2 keeps `valid_from`, `valid_to` and `is_current` columns: ```sql CREATE TABLE dim_customer_scd2 ( customer_sk INTEGER, customer_id INTEGER, city VARCHAR, valid_from DATE, valid_to DATE, is_current BOOLEAN ); INSERT INTO dim_customer_scd2 VALUES (1, 7, 'Mumbai', DATE '2024-01-01', DATE '9999-12-31', TRUE), (2, 8, 'Delhi', DATE '2024-01-01', DATE '9999-12-31', TRUE); CREATE TABLE incoming(customer_id INTEGER, city VARCHAR); INSERT INTO incoming VALUES (7, 'Pune'), (8, 'Delhi'), (9, 'Goa'); -- 1. Close current rows whose tracked value changed UPDATE dim_customer_scd2 d SET valid_to = DATE '2025-07-01', is_current = FALSE FROM incoming i WHERE d.customer_id = i.customer_id AND d.is_current AND d.city IS DISTINCT FROM i.city; -- 2. Insert a new current row for changed and brand-new customers INSERT INTO dim_customer_scd2 SELECT (SELECT MAX(customer_sk) FROM dim_customer_scd2) + ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY i.customer_id), i.customer_id, i.city, DATE '2025-07-01', DATE '9999-12-31', TRUE FROM incoming i LEFT JOIN dim_customer_scd2 d ON d.customer_id = i.customer_id AND d.is_current WHERE d.customer_id IS NULL; SELECT * FROM dim_customer_scd2 ORDER BY customer_id, valid_from; ``` Customer 7 now has two rows, Mumbai until 1 July and Pune from 1 July; customer 8 is unchanged; customer 9 is new. The old row's `valid_to` equals the new row's `valid_from`, and the end is exclusive, the same half-open rule as chapter 3, so every day belongs to exactly one version. A fact row joins to the version that was current on its date: ```sql norun SELECT f.order_id, d.city FROM fact_orders f JOIN dim_customer_scd2 d ON d.customer_id = f.customer_id AND f.order_date >= d.valid_from AND f.order_date < d.valid_to; ``` On Delta Lake the two steps become one MERGE, which the Pro project 1 builds end to end. dbt snapshots (handbook 11) and Databricks' `APPLY CHANGES` automate the same logic. ## Other patterns you'll meet - **Factless fact:** rows with keys and no measures, such as "student attended class". You count them. - **Periodic snapshot:** one row per entity per period, such as daily inventory or month-end balances. - **Accumulating snapshot:** one row per process instance, updated as it moves through stages (ordered, packed, shipped, delivered), with a date column per stage. - **Junk dimension:** a handful of low-cardinality flags (is_gift, is_express) combined into one small dimension. - **One Big Table:** a fully denormalised wide table. Popular on lakehouses because storage is cheap and joins are expensive. Build it from a clean star, not instead of one. ## Common mistakes - **No stated grain.** Ask "what is one row?" before writing any SQL. - **Summing a ratio or a balance.** - **SCD2 change detection with `<>`.** NULL-to-value changes are missed. Use IS DISTINCT FROM. - **Overlapping SCD2 ranges** for one key. Test that each key has exactly one current row and no gaps. - **Joining facts to the current dimension row** when the report needs history. ## In the interview **"Design a data model for a food-delivery app."** State the business questions, then the grain of each fact (one row per order, one per delivery event), the dimensions (customer, restaurant, rider, date, location), which dimensions need SCD2 (restaurant commission rate, customer city), and how it will be loaded. Grain first, out loud. **"SCD Type 1 vs Type 2?"** Overwrite versus keep history with validity dates. Mention surrogate keys, the current flag, and IS DISTINCT FROM for change detection. ```quiz A fact table has one row per order, and someone adds daily total rows to it. What breaks? - Nothing * Every SUM double counts, because the table mixes two grains - Joins to dimensions stop working > One table, one grain. Daily totals belong in their own aggregate table. --- Which measure is semi-additive? - Order amount * Account balance at the end of each day - Number of clicks > Balances can be summed across accounts on one day, but not across days. --- Why does SCD Type 2 need a surrogate key? * The same customer_id appears in several rows, one per version, so it can't be the primary key - Surrogate keys are faster to type - The source system requires it > Each version needs its own key so facts can point at the version current at the time. ```

title: Views, materialized views and temporary objects
md:
By the end of this chapter you can choose between a view, a materialized view, a table and a temp table for any piece of logic, and you know what each one costs when the data grows. ## Four ways to save a query | Object | Stores data? | Fresh? | Cost | |---|---|---|---| | View | no, just the SQL | always, recomputed on every read | every query pays the full compute | | Materialized view | yes | refreshed on a schedule or incrementally | storage plus refresh | | Table (built by a job) | yes | as fresh as the last job run | storage plus the job | | Temp table | yes, for this session only | as of when you created it | gone when the session ends | ## Views ```sql CREATE VIEW v_delivered_orders AS SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_ts, quantity * unit_price AS gross FROM shop_orders WHERE status = 'delivered'; SELECT date_trunc('month', order_ts) AS month, SUM(gross) AS gross FROM v_delivered_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-10-01' GROUP BY month ORDER BY month; ``` A view gives logic a name and one place to change it. The optimiser merges the view's SQL into your query, so the outer filter still prunes data. Good uses: - One agreed definition, such as "a delivered order", that everyone queries. - Hiding columns or rows for security: a view that leaves out email and phone. - A stable interface: rename a source column underneath, and the view keeps the old name. Watch for views built on views built on views. Each layer looks cheap, but the final query can be enormous and slow, and nobody can read it. ## Materialized views A materialized view stores its result and refreshes it: ```sql norun CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_daily_sales AS SELECT CAST(order_ts AS DATE) AS day, channel, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross FROM shop_orders GROUP BY ALL; ``` Reads are fast because the work is done in advance. Engines differ a lot: Snowflake and BigQuery refresh automatically with restrictions on the SQL allowed; Databricks materialized views refresh in a Lakeflow pipeline and can update incrementally; Postgres needs an explicit `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`. DuckDB doesn't have them, which is why this block doesn't run here. Check the engine's limits before relying on one. In practice many teams skip materialized views and build a gold table with a scheduled job or a dbt model, which gives them full control over refresh, testing and backfills. ## Temp tables ```sql CREATE TEMP TABLE big_spenders AS SELECT customer_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross FROM shop_orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(quantity * unit_price) > 3000000; SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers, ROUND(AVG(gross)) AS avg_gross FROM big_spenders; ``` A temp table holds an intermediate result for the rest of your session: compute once, query many times, inspect while debugging. In Spark, `df.createOrReplaceTempView('name')` gives a DataFrame a name for SQL, but it's a view, not stored data. Add `.cache()` if you'll reuse it (handbook 5). ## Choosing - Logic used in one query: a CTE (chapter 7). - Logic shared by many queries and cheap to compute: a view. - Expensive logic read many times: a table built by a job, or a materialized view if the engine's refresh fits. - Scratch work in one session: a temp table. ## Common mistakes - **A view over a 1-billion-row table** queried by a dashboard every minute. Every refresh pays for the full scan. - **`SELECT *` in a view.** In some engines the column list is fixed when the view is created, so new source columns don't appear, or a dropped column breaks the view. - **Expecting a temp table to exist in the next job.** It's gone when the session ends. - **Deep view chains** nobody can debug. ## In the interview **"View vs materialized view?"** A view stores only SQL and recomputes on every read; a materialized view stores the result and refreshes it. Trade freshness and compute against storage and staleness, and name the engine's refresh behaviour. **"CTE vs temp table?"** A CTE lives in one query and may be recomputed; a temp table lives for the session and is computed once. ```quiz A dashboard reads a view over a 2-billion-row table 500 times a day. What's the main problem? - Views can't be read that often * Every read recomputes the full query, paying for the scan each time - The view will go out of date > Precompute: a gold table built by a job, or a materialized view. --- Which object disappears when your session ends? - A view - A materialized view * A temp table > Temp tables are session-scoped. Views and materialized views are saved in the catalog. --- What does `df.createOrReplaceTempView('orders')` do in Spark? * Gives the DataFrame a name you can query with SQL in this session - Writes the data to disk - Creates a permanent table > It's a named view of the DataFrame's plan, not stored data. Use cache() or a table to store it. ```

title: Transactions and consistency
md:
By the end of this chapter you can explain ACID in plain words, group statements into a transaction, describe isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent, and explain how lakehouse formats like Delta Lake bring transactions to files. ## Why a DE cares A load that deletes yesterday's rows and then crashes before inserting the new ones leaves a hole in every report. A reader that sees half of a big update shows numbers that never existed. Transactions are how databases stop that, and table formats like Delta Lake and Iceberg exist largely to bring the same guarantees to files in cloud storage. ## ACID in plain words | Letter | Promise | Without it | |---|---|---| | Atomicity | all of a transaction happens, or none of it | half-finished loads | | Consistency | constraints hold before and after | orphan rows, duplicate keys | | Isolation | concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work | reports reading partial data | | Durability | once committed, it survives a crash | "successful" loads that vanish | ## A transaction ```sql CREATE TABLE accounts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, owner VARCHAR, balance DECIMAL(12, 2)); INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, 'Asha', 5000), (2, 'Ravi', 1000); BEGIN TRANSACTION; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 700 WHERE id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 700 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT; SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY id; ``` Both updates commit together. Now a failure: ```sql CREATE TABLE accounts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, owner VARCHAR, balance DECIMAL(12, 2)); INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, 'Asha', 5000), (2, 'Ravi', 1000); BEGIN TRANSACTION; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 700 WHERE id = 1; -- something goes wrong here, so we undo everything since BEGIN ROLLBACK; SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY id; ``` Asha keeps her ₹5,000. In application code, the pattern is: begin, do the work, commit if everything succeeded, roll back on any error. ## Isolation levels and anomalies When two transactions run at the same time, these things can go wrong: - **Dirty read:** reading another transaction's uncommitted change, which may be rolled back. - **Non-repeatable read:** reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values. - **Phantom read:** running the same query twice and getting extra rows that someone inserted in between. - **Lost update:** two transactions read a value, both change it, and one overwrites the other. | Level | Prevents | Common default in | |---|---|---| | Read uncommitted | nothing | rarely used | | Read committed | dirty reads | Postgres, SQL Server, Oracle | | Repeatable read | + non-repeatable reads | MySQL InnoDB | | Serializable | everything: as if run one at a time | strictest, slowest | | Snapshot isolation | readers see a consistent snapshot as of their start | Delta Lake, Iceberg, Snowflake, DuckDB | Most analytics engines use snapshot isolation through **multi-version concurrency control (MVCC)**: writers create new versions, readers keep reading the version that was current when they started. Readers never block writers and never see half a load. ## Transactions on a lakehouse Plain Parquet files in a folder have no transactions. If a Spark job writing 200 files dies after 120, readers see 120 files. Delta Lake fixes this with a transaction log (`_delta_log`): a write adds files and then records one commit entry listing them. Readers only trust files named in committed log entries, so a half-finished write is invisible. That log also gives you: - **Time travel:** `SELECT * FROM t VERSION AS OF 12` or `TIMESTAMP AS OF '2025-06-01'`. - **Rollback:** `RESTORE TABLE t TO VERSION AS OF 12` after a bad load. - **Concurrent writers:** optimistic concurrency. Two jobs writing to different partitions both succeed; two changing the same files conflict, and one retries. ```sql norun DESCRIBE HISTORY silver.orders; -- who changed what, when SELECT COUNT(*) FROM silver.orders VERSION AS OF 41; -- the table before the bad load RESTORE TABLE silver.orders TO VERSION AS OF 41; -- undo it ``` These run on Databricks and on Spark with Delta. Iceberg has the same ideas with snapshots. ## Constraints Constraints let the database refuse bad data: ```sql CREATE TABLE orders_clean ( order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL, quantity INTEGER CHECK (quantity > 0), status VARCHAR CHECK (status IN ('placed', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'cancelled', 'returned')) ); INSERT INTO orders_clean VALUES (1, 10, 2, 'delivered'); SELECT * FROM orders_clean; ``` Try inserting `(2, 10, 0, 'delivered')` and it's rejected. Many warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks) accept PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY declarations but don't enforce them; they're hints for the optimiser and for documentation. Delta Lake enforces NOT NULL and CHECK constraints. So on a warehouse, uniqueness is your pipeline's job: test it (chapter 18). ## Common mistakes - **Delete and insert outside a transaction.** A crash in between leaves a gap. - **Assuming the warehouse enforces primary keys.** Usually it doesn't. - **Long transactions** holding locks in an OLTP source while you extract. Read from a replica or use CDC. - **Writing plain Parquet** from several jobs into one folder. Use a table format. ## In the interview **"Explain ACID."** One plain sentence per letter, with a pipeline example for atomicity: "if my load fails halfway, readers still see yesterday's complete table." **"How does Delta Lake give ACID on cloud storage?"** A transaction log of ordered commits. Readers only see files in committed entries; writers use optimistic concurrency; the log enables time travel and RESTORE. ```quiz A load deletes old rows, then crashes before inserting new ones. Which ACID property would have prevented the gap? * Atomicity - Durability - Consistency > Inside one transaction, the delete and insert commit together or not at all. --- What does snapshot isolation guarantee a reader? - It sees every change as soon as it is written * It sees a consistent version of the data as of when it started, never half a write - It blocks all writers > MVCC keeps old versions for readers while writers create new ones. --- On most cloud warehouses, what does a declared PRIMARY KEY do? - Rejects duplicate rows * Documents the key and helps the optimiser, but duplicates are still accepted - Creates an index that sorts the table > Test uniqueness in the pipeline instead of trusting the constraint. ```

title: Query performance
md:
By the end of this chapter you can read a query plan, find where the time goes, and apply the handful of fixes that solve most slow queries on warehouses and lakehouses: read less data, shuffle less data, and do less work twice. ## How analytical engines spend time Columnar engines (DuckDB, Spark, Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks SQL, Synapse) store each column separately, compressed, in files split into chunks with min/max statistics. Almost every speed-up comes from three ideas: 1. **Read less:** fewer columns, fewer files, fewer row groups. 2. **Move less:** shuffles and big joins are the expensive steps on a cluster. 3. **Compute once:** don't recompute the same heavy result for every query. ## Read the plan ```sql EXPLAIN SELECT channel, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-12-01' GROUP BY channel; ``` `EXPLAIN` shows the plan the optimiser chose without running it. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs it and adds the real time and row count per step: ```sql EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT channel, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-12-01' GROUP BY channel; ``` Read it bottom up: the scan, then the filter, then the aggregate. Look for three things: the step with the most time, a step whose row count is far larger than you expected (a fan-out join or a missing filter), and a filter that runs after the scan instead of inside it. In Spark the same information is in `df.explain('formatted')` and the SQL tab of the Spark UI (handbook 5). ## Fix 1: select only the columns you need ```sql -- Reads every column of a million rows SELECT * FROM shop_orders WHERE status = 'returned' LIMIT 5; -- Reads two columns SELECT order_id, order_ts FROM shop_orders WHERE status = 'returned' LIMIT 5; ``` In a columnar store, unread columns are never touched on disk. On BigQuery and Synapse serverless you're billed by bytes scanned, so `SELECT *` is literally more expensive. ## Fix 2: let filters skip data Engines skip files and row groups whose min/max statistics can't match your filter, and they skip whole folders when a table is partitioned by the filtered column. That only works when the filter is on the raw column: ```sql -- Can skip: compares the stored column to constants SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-12-01' AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01'; -- Harder to skip: a function wraps the column SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shop_orders WHERE strftime(order_ts, '%Y-%m') = '2025-12'; ``` Both return the same count. The first form lets the engine prune; the second makes it compute the function for every row first. Write filters as ranges on the stored column. **Partitioning** splits a table into folders by a column, usually a date. Pick a column almost every query filters on, with a manageable number of values: daily partitions over years is fine, partitioning by customer_id creates millions of tiny folders and is far slower. On Delta, **Z-ordering** or **liquid clustering** co-locate rows by a second column so file skipping works on it too. ## Fix 3: join smart - **Filter and aggregate before joining.** Shrink both sides first. - **Broadcast small tables.** Copying a 5,000-row product table to every worker avoids shuffling a billion-row fact. Spark does it automatically below a size threshold and accepts a `BROADCAST` hint. - **Join on the same types.** A string key against an integer key forces a cast on every row. - **Watch for skew.** If one customer has 30% of the orders, one task does 30% of the work. Spark's adaptive query execution (AQE) splits skewed partitions; salting the key is the manual fix. ```sql WITH small_orders AS ( SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-12-01' GROUP BY product_id ) SELECT p.category, SUM(s.gross) AS gross FROM small_orders s JOIN shop_products p ON p.product_id = s.product_id GROUP BY p.category ORDER BY gross DESC; ``` The fact is aggregated to 5,000 rows before it meets the product table. ## Fix 4: compute once - A heavy CTE referenced three times: materialise it (chapter 7). - A dashboard query run every minute over raw data: build a gold aggregate table (chapter 15). - Spark DataFrames reused in several actions: `cache()` them, then `unpersist()`. ## Fix 5: keep files healthy Lakehouse tables slow down when they collect thousands of tiny files from streaming or frequent small appends. Each file costs a request and a footer read. Compact them with `OPTIMIZE` on Delta (or auto-compaction), aim for files of roughly 100 MB to 1 GB, and clean up old versions with `VACUUM` after your time travel window. ## A debugging routine When someone says "this query got slow": 1. Did the data grow, or did the query or plan change? Compare row counts and the plan with last week's. 2. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Find the slowest step and the biggest row count. 3. Check filters are prunable and columns are selected, not starred. 4. Check join row counts for fan-out, and key types. 5. Check for skew and small files. 6. Only then add resources. A bigger cluster for a bad plan just burns more money faster. ## Common mistakes - **`SELECT *` in production queries.** - **Functions on filtered columns** that block pruning. - **Over-partitioning** into millions of small folders. - **DISTINCT to fix a fan-out** instead of fixing the join. - **Scaling the cluster first.** ## In the interview **"A query got slow. How do you debug it?"** Walk through the routine above, in order, and name one concrete fix for each finding. Practice 78 is this question. **"Why does this query scan the whole table?"** Usually a function around the partition or filter column, an implicit cast, or `SELECT *`. Rewrite as a range on the raw column. Practice 69 asks exactly this. ```quiz Which filter lets the engine skip partitions of a table partitioned by order_date? - `WHERE year(order_date) = 2025` * `WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND order_date < '2026-01-01'` - `WHERE CAST(order_date AS VARCHAR) LIKE '2025%'` > Compare the raw column with constants. A function or cast around it hides it from pruning. --- A 2-billion-row fact joins a 5,000-row product table in Spark. What's the usual best strategy? - Sort-merge join * Broadcast the product table - Cross join > Copying the small table to every executor avoids shuffling the huge one. --- A query slowed down after a month of streaming writes into a Delta table. What's a likely cause? - The SQL changed * Thousands of small files; compact them with OPTIMIZE - Delta tables slow down with age > Many tiny files mean many reads and footers. Compaction restores large files. ```

title: Data quality with SQL
md:
By the end of this chapter you can write the core data quality checks in SQL, reconcile a load against its source, quarantine bad rows instead of loading them, and explain the write-audit-publish pattern. ## Why quality is a DE job Nobody notices a pipeline that works. Everyone notices the morning the revenue dashboard shows double. Most data incidents are not crashes: the job succeeds and the data is wrong. Checks catch that before a stakeholder does. ## The six checks that catch most problems | Check | Question | Example on our tables | |---|---|---| | Volume | did roughly the expected number of rows arrive? | orders today vs the 7-day average | | Uniqueness | is the key unique? | one row per order_id | | Completeness | are required columns filled? | no NULL customer_id | | Validity | are values in range and format? | quantity > 0, status in the known list | | Referential integrity | do foreign keys point at real rows? | every order's customer exists | | Freshness | is the data recent enough? | latest order_ts within the last hour | ## Uniqueness and completeness ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows, COUNT(DISTINCT event_id) AS distinct_keys, COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT event_id) AS duplicate_rows, COUNT(*) - COUNT(user_id) AS null_user_id, ROUND(100.0 * (COUNT(*) - COUNT(user_id)) / COUNT(*), 2) AS null_user_pct FROM web_events; ``` One pass, several checks. For web events, anonymous users are expected, so the right check isn't "zero NULLs" but "NULL rate between 15% and 25%". A good check encodes what normal looks like. ## Validity ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE distance_km <= 0) AS zero_or_negative_distance, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE fare < 0) AS negative_fare, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE dropoff_ts <= pickup_ts) AS ends_before_start, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE passengers NOT BETWEEN 1 AND 6) AS odd_passenger_count, COUNT(*) AS trips FROM taxi_trips; ``` ## Referential integrity ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS orphan_orders FROM shop_orders o WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM shop_customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id); ``` Zero here. In real systems orphans often appear because facts arrive before their dimension rows. Common fixes: load dimensions first, or point late facts at an "Unknown" dimension member and repair them when the dimension row arrives. ## Volume against history ```sql WITH daily AS ( SELECT CAST(order_ts AS DATE) AS day, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-11-01' GROUP BY day ), scored AS ( SELECT day, orders, AVG(orders) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 7 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) AS avg_prev_7 FROM daily ) SELECT day, orders, ROUND(avg_prev_7) AS avg_prev_7, ROUND(100.0 * (orders - avg_prev_7) / avg_prev_7, 1) AS pct_vs_avg, ABS(orders - avg_prev_7) > 0.3 * avg_prev_7 AS alert FROM scored WHERE avg_prev_7 IS NOT NULL ORDER BY day LIMIT 15; ``` A fixed threshold ("at least 1,000 rows") breaks on festival days and weekends. Comparing with recent history adapts. Seasonal businesses compare with the same weekday in previous weeks. ## Reconciliation After a load, prove the target matches the source: ```sql WITH source AS ( SELECT CAST(order_ts AS DATE) AS day, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-12-01' AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-12-08' GROUP BY day ), target AS ( -- pretend the load lost a few rows on one day SELECT CAST(order_ts AS DATE) AS day, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-12-01' AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-12-08' AND NOT (CAST(order_ts AS DATE) = DATE '2025-12-05' AND order_id % 100 = 0) GROUP BY day ) SELECT s.day, s.n AS source_rows, t.n AS target_rows, s.n - t.n AS missing, s.gross - t.gross AS gross_diff FROM source s FULL JOIN target t ON t.day = s.day WHERE s.n IS DISTINCT FROM t.n OR s.gross IS DISTINCT FROM t.gross ORDER BY s.day; ``` Counts and sums per day narrow a problem to one partition fast; chapter 8's EXCEPT then finds the exact rows. ## Quarantine instead of failing or loading Bad rows have three possible fates: fail the whole job, load them anyway, or set them aside. For most pipelines, setting aside is best: ```sql CREATE TABLE trips_clean AS SELECT * FROM taxi_trips WHERE distance_km > 0 AND fare >= 0 AND dropoff_ts > pickup_ts; CREATE TABLE trips_quarantine AS SELECT *, CASE WHEN distance_km <= 0 THEN 'zero_or_negative_distance' WHEN fare < 0 THEN 'negative_fare' ELSE 'ends_before_start' END AS reason FROM taxi_trips WHERE NOT (distance_km > 0 AND fare >= 0 AND dropoff_ts > pickup_ts); SELECT reason, COUNT(*) AS rows FROM trips_quarantine GROUP BY reason ORDER BY rows DESC; ``` Then alert when the quarantine rate is unusually high. A few bad rows are normal; 20% means a source broke and the job should stop. ## Write, audit, publish The safest pattern for important tables: 1. **Write** the new data to a staging table or a hidden branch, not the table people read. 2. **Audit** it with the checks above. 3. **Publish** only if checks pass: swap or merge into production in one transaction. If an audit fails, consumers keep seeing yesterday's correct data instead of today's wrong data. Delta Lake (with a staging table or shallow clone), Iceberg (with branches) and dbt (build, test, then swap) all support it. ## Tools You can write all of this in SQL, and you should be able to in an interview. In production, teams use dbt tests (handbook 11), Great Expectations or Soda for expectation suites, Databricks Lakeflow expectations, and data contracts that make the source team agree to a schema and rules. ## Common mistakes - **Checks that only test "not NULL" and "unique".** Volume and freshness catch more real incidents. - **Hard-coded thresholds** that alert every weekend until everyone ignores them. - **Failing the whole pipeline for one bad row.** - **Checking only after publishing.** People already saw the bad numbers. - **No owner for an alert.** Every check needs a person who acts on it. ## In the interview **"What data quality checks do you put on a pipeline?"** Name the six with a concrete example each, then say where they run (before publish), what happens on failure (quarantine or block), and who gets alerted. **"Source and target counts don't match. What do you do?"** Narrow by partition with counts and sums, then EXCEPT both ways on the failing partition, then check filters, join fan-out, late data and dedup logic. ```quiz A job runs successfully but loads half the usual rows. Which check catches it? - Uniqueness * Volume compared with recent history - Referential integrity > Successful jobs with wrong data are the common incident. Volume and freshness checks find them. --- What is the point of write-audit-publish? * Readers keep seeing the last good data if the new data fails its checks - It makes loads faster - It removes the need for tests > New data is checked in staging and only swapped into production when it passes. --- 1 in 10,000 rows has a negative fare. What should most pipelines do? - Fail the whole job - Load them unchanged * Move them to a quarantine table with a reason, and alert if the rate jumps > Quarantine keeps good data flowing and keeps bad rows for investigation. ```

title: Dialect cheat sheet
md:
By the end of this chapter you can translate a query between the engines Indian DE job descriptions ask for most: Spark SQL on Databricks, Snowflake, BigQuery, SQL Server and Synapse, and Postgres. Standard SQL covers about 90% of a query; this chapter is the other 10%. ## How to use this page Write standard SQL first: SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, window functions and CTEs work everywhere. When something fails on a new engine, it's almost always one of the rows below. Versions matter: where a feature arrived recently, the version is noted. When in doubt, check the engine's docs for your version. ## Querying | Task | Spark SQL / Databricks | Snowflake | BigQuery | SQL Server / Synapse | Postgres | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | First n rows | `LIMIT n` | `LIMIT n` or `TOP n` | `LIMIT n` | `TOP n`, or `OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT n ROWS ONLY` | `LIMIT n` | | Quote a name | `` `my col` `` | `"my col"` | `` `my col` `` | `[my col]` | `"my col"` | | Filter on a window | `QUALIFY` on Databricks; subquery in older open-source Spark | `QUALIFY` | `QUALIFY` | subquery | subquery | | Group by all non-aggregates | `GROUP BY ALL` on Databricks | `GROUP BY ALL` | `GROUP BY ALL` | list the columns | list the columns | | Integer `7 / 2` | `3.5` (`7 div 2` is 3) | `3.5` | `3.5` (`DIV(7, 2)` is 3) | `3` | `3` | | Safe divide | `try_divide(a, b)` | `DIV0NULL(a, b)` | `SAFE_DIVIDE(a, b)` | `a / NULLIF(b, 0)` | `a / NULLIF(b, 0)` | | Cast that returns NULL on failure | `try_cast(x AS INT)` | `TRY_CAST(x AS INT)` | `SAFE_CAST(x AS INT64)` | `TRY_CAST(x AS INT)` | no built-in: use a CASE with a regex check | ## NULLs and strings | Task | Spark SQL / Databricks | Snowflake | BigQuery | SQL Server / Synapse | Postgres | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Default for NULL | `coalesce`, `nvl` | `COALESCE`, `NVL`, `IFNULL` | `COALESCE`, `IFNULL` | `COALESCE`, `ISNULL` | `COALESCE` | | Null-safe equals | `a <=> b`, `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` | `EQUAL_NULL(a, b)`, `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` | `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` | `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` (2022+) | `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` | | Concatenate | `concat(a, b)`, `a \|\| b` | `a \|\| b`, `CONCAT` | `CONCAT`, `a \|\| b` | `a + b`, `CONCAT` | `a \|\| b` | | Regex extract | `regexp_extract(s, pat, 1)` | `REGEXP_SUBSTR(s, pat)` | `REGEXP_EXTRACT(s, pat)` | limited: `PATINDEX`; regex functions arrive in SQL Server 2025 | `substring(s from pat)`, `regexp_match` | | Split to array | `split(s, ',')` | `SPLIT(s, ',')` | `SPLIT(s, ',')` | `STRING_SPLIT(s, ',')` returns rows | `string_to_array(s, ',')` | | Rows to text | `concat_ws(',', collect_list(x))` | `LISTAGG(x, ',')` | `STRING_AGG(x, ',')` | `STRING_AGG(x, ',')` | `string_agg(x, ',')` | ## Dates | Task | Spark SQL / Databricks | Snowflake | BigQuery | SQL Server / Synapse | Postgres | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Now | `current_timestamp()` | `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` | `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()` | `SYSDATETIME()`, `GETDATE()` | `now()` | | Add days | `date_add(d, 7)` | `DATEADD(day, 7, d)` | `DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 7 DAY)` | `DATEADD(day, 7, d)` | `d + INTERVAL '7 days'` | | Add months | `add_months(d, 1)` | `DATEADD(month, 1, d)` | `DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 1 MONTH)` | `DATEADD(month, 1, d)` | `d + INTERVAL '1 month'` | | Days between | `datediff(end, start)` | `DATEDIFF(day, start, end)` | `DATE_DIFF(end, start, DAY)` | `DATEDIFF(day, start, end)` | `end - start` | | Start of month | `date_trunc('MONTH', ts)` | `DATE_TRUNC('month', ts)` | `DATE_TRUNC(d, MONTH)` | `DATETRUNC(month, d)` (2022+) | `date_trunc('month', ts)` | | Parse text | `to_date(s, 'dd/MM/yyyy')` | `TO_DATE(s, 'DD/MM/YYYY')` | `PARSE_DATE('%d/%m/%Y', s)` | `CONVERT(date, s, 103)` | `to_date(s, 'DD/MM/YYYY')` | | Series of dates | `explode(sequence(start, end, interval 1 day))` | `GENERATOR` with `DATEADD` | `UNNEST(GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY(start, end))` | `GENERATE_SERIES` (2022+), or a recursive CTE | `generate_series(start, end, '1 day')` | Watch the argument order in date differences: Spark and BigQuery put the end first, Snowflake and SQL Server put the unit and start first. ## Loading and nested data | Task | Spark SQL / Databricks | Snowflake | BigQuery | SQL Server / Synapse | Postgres | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Upsert | `MERGE INTO` (Delta) | `MERGE` | `MERGE` | `MERGE` | `MERGE` (15+), `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` | | Replace a table | `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE` | `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE` | `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE` | `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` then create | `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` then create | | Explode an array | `explode(arr)`, `LATERAL VIEW` | `LATERAL FLATTEN(input => arr)` | `CROSS JOIN UNNEST(arr)` | `CROSS APPLY OPENJSON(json)` | `unnest(arr)` | | JSON field | `get_json_object(j, '$.a')`, `j:a` | `j:a` on VARIANT | `JSON_VALUE(j, '$.a')` | `JSON_VALUE(j, '$.a')` | `j ->> 'a'` | | Set difference | `EXCEPT` | `EXCEPT`, `MINUS` | `EXCEPT DISTINCT` | `EXCEPT` | `EXCEPT` | | Approximate distinct | `approx_count_distinct` | `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` | `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` | `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` (2019+) | extension needed | | Time travel | `VERSION AS OF n` (Delta) | `AT(OFFSET => -60)` | `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF ts` | temporal tables | not built in | ## The same query in two dialects Monthly revenue and month-over-month growth, Spark SQL: ```sql norun SELECT month, revenue, ROUND(100 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS mom_pct FROM ( SELECT date_trunc('MONTH', order_ts) AS month, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS revenue FROM silver.orders GROUP BY date_trunc('MONTH', order_ts) ) m ORDER BY month; ``` SQL Server: ```sql norun SELECT month, revenue, ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 1) AS mom_pct FROM ( SELECT DATETRUNC(month, order_ts) AS month, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS revenue FROM dbo.orders GROUP BY DATETRUNC(month, order_ts) ) m ORDER BY month; ``` Two differences: the date-truncation syntax, and `100.0` plus NULLIF, because SQL Server does integer division and errors on divide by zero. ## Common mistakes - **Assuming `/` means the same everywhere.** - **Swapped date-diff arguments** between Spark and Snowflake. - **Writing QUALIFY for SQL Server or Postgres.** - **Backticks in Snowflake** or double quotes in Spark: in Spark, double quotes mean a string. ## In the interview **"Which SQL dialects have you used?"** Name them and one real difference you hit, such as "SQL Server's integer division broke a ratio when we migrated to Synapse, so we standardised on multiplying by 100.0." A specific story beats a list. ```quiz `SELECT 7 / 2` in SQL Server returns what? * 3 - 3.5 - An error > Integer divided by integer is integer division in SQL Server and Postgres. Spark, Snowflake and BigQuery return 3.5. --- In Spark SQL, what does `WHERE city = "Pune"` compare against? * The string Pune, because Spark treats double quotes as a string by default - A column called Pune - Nothing, it's a syntax error > Spark uses backticks for names. Snowflake and Postgres use double quotes for names, so the same line means something else there. --- Which engine needs a subquery instead of QUALIFY to filter on ROW_NUMBER()? - Snowflake - BigQuery * Postgres > Postgres and SQL Server don't support QUALIFY. Wrap the window in a subquery and filter outside. ```

title: Pattern library
md:
By the end of this chapter you have a toolbox of the SQL patterns that solve most real pipeline and interview problems, each one runnable on the Playground tables. Most real transformation work is a few of these combined at the right grain. ## Latest row per key The dedup that every CDC feed and every bronze-to-silver job needs. Order by the change time, then a tie-breaker: ```sql SELECT * FROM web_events QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC, session_id DESC) = 1 LIMIT 10; ``` ## Change detection between two snapshots Classify every key as inserted, deleted, updated or unchanged by comparing a hash of the tracked columns: ```sql WITH yesterday(id, name, city) AS (VALUES (1, 'Asha', 'Pune'), (2, 'Ravi', 'Delhi'), (3, 'Meera', 'Goa')), today(id, name, city) AS (VALUES (1, 'Asha', 'Pune'), (2, 'Ravi', 'Mumbai'), (4, 'Kabir', 'Kochi')), y AS (SELECT id, md5(concat_ws('|', name, city)) AS h FROM yesterday), t AS (SELECT id, md5(concat_ws('|', name, city)) AS h FROM today) SELECT COALESCE(t.id, y.id) AS id, CASE WHEN y.id IS NULL THEN 'INSERT' WHEN t.id IS NULL THEN 'DELETE' WHEN t.h <> y.h THEN 'UPDATE' ELSE 'SAME' END AS change_type FROM t FULL JOIN y ON y.id = t.id ORDER BY id; ``` `concat_ws` skips NULLs, so `('a', NULL)` and `(NULL, 'a')` would hash the same. In production, wrap each column in `COALESCE(col, '~')` before hashing. ## Fill missing days per group ```sql WITH days AS ( SELECT CAST(d AS DATE) AS day FROM generate_series(TIMESTAMP '2025-12-01', TIMESTAMP '2025-12-07', INTERVAL 1 DAY) t(d) ), channels AS (SELECT DISTINCT channel FROM shop_orders), sales AS ( SELECT CAST(order_ts AS DATE) AS day, channel, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-12-01' AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-12-08' AND status = 'returned' AND quantity = 6 GROUP BY ALL ) SELECT d.day, c.channel, COALESCE(s.orders, 0) AS orders FROM days d CROSS JOIN channels c LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.day = d.day AND s.channel = c.channel ORDER BY d.day, c.channel; ``` ## Sessionise clicks A new session starts after 30 minutes of inactivity. Flag the starts with LAG, then running-sum the flags: ```sql WITH clicks AS ( SELECT user_id, event_ts FROM web_events WHERE user_id = 42 ), flagged AS ( SELECT user_id, event_ts, CASE WHEN LAG(event_ts) OVER w IS NULL OR event_ts - LAG(event_ts) OVER w > INTERVAL 30 MINUTE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session FROM clicks WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) ) SELECT user_id, SUM(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) AS session_no, event_ts FROM flagged ORDER BY event_ts LIMIT 15; ``` "Flag a change, then cumulative sum" is a general trick: it also groups consecutive status runs and price periods. ## Funnel conversion ```sql WITH per_session AS ( SELECT session_id, MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'page_view' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS viewed, MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'add_to_cart' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS carted, MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'checkout' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS checked_out, MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'purchase' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS purchased FROM web_events GROUP BY session_id ) SELECT SUM(viewed) AS viewed, SUM(carted) AS carted, SUM(checked_out) AS checked_out, SUM(purchased) AS purchased, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(purchased) / NULLIF(SUM(viewed), 0), 2) AS view_to_purchase_pct FROM per_session; ``` A strict funnel also requires the steps in order; compare the timestamps of each step per session for that. ## Forward fill the last known value ```sql WITH readings(device, ts, temp) AS ( VALUES ('d1', 1, 30.5), ('d1', 2, NULL), ('d1', 3, NULL), ('d1', 4, 31.0), ('d1', 5, NULL) ) SELECT device, ts, temp, LAST_VALUE(temp IGNORE NULLS) OVER (PARTITION BY device ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS temp_filled FROM readings ORDER BY ts; ``` Spark writes it `last(temp, true)`; Snowflake and BigQuery use `IGNORE NULLS` as here. ## Year over year ```sql WITH m AS ( SELECT date_trunc('month', order_ts) AS month, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS revenue FROM shop_orders GROUP BY month ) SELECT cur.month, cur.revenue, prev.revenue AS revenue_last_year, ROUND(100.0 * (cur.revenue - prev.revenue) / NULLIF(prev.revenue, 0), 1) AS yoy_pct FROM m cur LEFT JOIN m prev ON prev.month = cur.month - INTERVAL 1 YEAR WHERE cur.month >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01' ORDER BY cur.month; ``` A self join on "same month last year" is clearer than `LAG(revenue, 12)`, which silently compares the wrong months if one month is missing. ## Point-in-time join Attach the version of a dimension that was valid when the fact happened (chapter 14): ```sql WITH dim(customer_id, city, valid_from, valid_to) AS ( VALUES (7, 'Mumbai', DATE '2024-01-01', DATE '2025-07-01'), (7, 'Pune', DATE '2025-07-01', DATE '9999-12-31') ), facts(order_id, customer_id, order_date) AS ( VALUES (1, 7, DATE '2025-03-10'), (2, 7, DATE '2025-07-01'), (3, 7, DATE '2025-09-20') ) SELECT f.order_id, f.order_date, d.city FROM facts f JOIN dim d ON d.customer_id = f.customer_id AND f.order_date >= d.valid_from AND f.order_date < d.valid_to ORDER BY f.order_id; ``` DuckDB also has `ASOF JOIN`, and Spark has a similar function for time series. The range join above works everywhere. ## Pairs bought together ```sql WITH baskets AS ( SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, product_id FROM shop_orders WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01' ) SELECT a.product_id AS product_a, b.product_id AS product_b, COUNT(*) AS together FROM baskets a JOIN baskets b ON b.customer_id = a.customer_id AND a.product_id < b.product_id GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY together DESC LIMIT 10; ``` Here a basket is everything a customer bought in 2025; in a real shop it would be one order or one session. `a.product_id < b.product_id` keeps each pair once and drops a product paired with itself. Self joins grow quickly, so filter to a small window first. ## Growth accounting Label every customer each month as new, retained, resurrected or churned. Handbook 13 builds the full report; the core is a comparison of this month's activity with the history: ```sql WITH active AS ( SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, date_trunc('month', order_ts) AS month FROM shop_orders WHERE customer_id <= 2000 ), labelled AS ( SELECT a.customer_id, a.month, MIN(a.month) OVER (PARTITION BY a.customer_id) AS first_month, LAG(a.month) OVER (PARTITION BY a.customer_id ORDER BY a.month) AS prev_active FROM active a ) SELECT month, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE month = first_month) AS new_customers, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE prev_active = month - INTERVAL 1 MONTH) AS retained, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE prev_active < month - INTERVAL 1 MONTH) AS resurrected FROM labelled GROUP BY month ORDER BY month LIMIT 12; ``` Churned customers are the ones active last month and missing this month, found with the anti join from chapter 10. ## How to use this toolbox When a new problem arrives, ask which patterns it combines. "Weekly active users who came back after a break, by city" is growth accounting plus a dimension join plus date truncation. Name the grain, pick the patterns, then write one CTE per step. ```quiz To dedupe a CDC feed to the latest row per key, what should the window ORDER BY include? - Only the key * The change timestamp descending, plus a tie-breaker - Nothing, ROW_NUMBER picks the newest > Without a tie-breaker, two rows with the same timestamp make the result change between runs. --- What does the "flag, then cumulative sum" trick do in sessionisation? * Turns session-start flags into a running session number for every click - Counts all clicks per user - Removes duplicate clicks > Each new-session flag increments the running sum, so all clicks in one session share a number. --- Why compare with the same month last year by a self join rather than LAG(revenue, 12)? - LAG is slower * If a month is missing, LAG(…, 12) compares against the wrong month - LAG doesn't work on dates > A join on the actual month value is always correct, even with gaps. ```
